Every reflection is conjugate to the reflection in the short root $e_1$, which fixes $\pm e_2,\pm e_3,\pm e_4$ and pairs the other eighteen vertices (shape $1^62^9$), or to the reflection in the long root $e_1-e_2$, which fixes $\pm e_3,\pm e_4$ and the eight half-vectors with equal first two signs (shape $1^{12}2^6$).

Item 3. The elements of $M_{24}$ of cycle shape $4^6$ form one conjugacy class (Conway and Sloane 1999). Fix such an element $a$ and put $z:=a^2$, of shape $2^{12}$. A quaternion subgroup containing $a$ contains an element $b$ with $b^2=z$ and $bab^{-1}=a^{-1}$, and then $b\in C_{M_{24}}(z)$. Exhaustive enumeration of $C_{M_{24}}(z)$, of order $7680$, gives $96$ elements inverting $a$, none of which has square $z$. Every nonidentity element of $Q_8^L$ or $Q_8^R$ has shape $2^{12}$, for $\epsilon=-1$, or $4^6$, for the six units of order four; an inclusion $\beta^{-1}Q_8^{L}\beta\le M_{24}$ or $\beta^{-1}Q_8^{R}\beta\le M_{24}$ would therefore contradict the first statement.

Item 4. The map $\tau$ equals $-1$ times the reflection in $e_3-e_4$, so it lies in $W(F_4)$; left and right multiplication by the unit $\omega$ preserve $V_{24}$ and are rotations in $W(F_4)$. With $q:=(j-k)/\sqrt2$ one has $\tau(x)=-q\bar xq^{-1}$, so $\tau^2=1$, and $q\bar\omega q^{-1}=\omega$ gives $\tau(\omega\,\tau(x))=x\omega$; conjugation by $\tau$ therefore interchanges $x\mapsto\omega x$ and $x\mapsto x\omega$. Hence $K_{18}=N\rtimes\langle\tau\rangle$ with $N:=\{x\mapsto\omega^ax\omega^b\}\cong C_3^2$. Since $\tau$ commutes with $x\mapsto\omega x\omega$ and inverts $x\mapsto\omega x\omega^{-1}$, $K_{18}=\langle x\mapsto\omega x\omega\rangle\times\langle x\mapsto\omega x\omega^{-1},\tau\rangle\cong C_3\times S_3$. By item 2, every $K_\beta$ is a subgroup of $W(F_4)$ contained in the set $\mathcal A$ of the $346$ qualifying elements. Exhaustive closure over $\mathcal A$ shows that every subgroup of $W(F_4)$ contained in $\mathcal A$ is generated by two elements of $\mathcal A$. These subgroups number $224$ and form $18$ conjugacy classes, of orders $1$, $2$ (two classes), $3$ (three classes), $4$, $6$ (four classes), $8$, $9$, $12$, $18$ and $24$ (three classes). The maximal members are the conjugates of $K_{18}$ and three classes of order $24$. A group in one of the latter has one involution and six elements of shape $4^6$, which together with the identity form its Sylow $2$-subgroup $Q_8^L$ or $Q_8^R$, so item 3 excludes all three classes, together with the class of order $8$, which consists of $Q_8^L$ and $Q_8^R$. The same enumeration places every remaining class inside a conjugate of $K_{18}$, $\langle c\rangle$ or $\langle g_6\rangle$, and shows that $\langle c\rangle$ and $\langle g_6\rangle$ lie only in groups of order $24$. The Coxeter element acts on the $24$ short roots in two orbits of length equal to the Coxeter number $12$, so it has shape $12^2$, and $g_6$ has shape $6^4$. Both shapes occur in $M_{24}$, so the cycle-matching bijection of item 2, written $\beta_c$ for $c$, places each cyclic group inside some $K_\beta$, and maximality gives equality. For $K_{18}$, realize $\Omega=\mathbb F_{23}\cup\{\infty\}$ and $\mathcal G_{24}$ as the binary span of $\mathbf 1_\Omega$ and the $23$ sets $(N_{23}+s)\cup\{\infty\}$, $s\in\mathbb F_{23}$, where $N_{23}=\{5,7,10,11,14,15,17,19,20,21,22\}$ is the set of quadratic non-residues modulo $23$; this code has parameters $[24,12,8]$ and represents the class of Theorem U.1. Define $\beta_{18}$ by
$$
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
v&1&-1&i&-i&j&-j&k&-k\\\hline
\beta_{18}^{-1}(v)&0&2&1&15&12&13&5&6
\end{array}
$$
and, writing $\frac12(\pm1\pm i\pm j\pm k)$ by its sign string,
$$
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
v&{+}{+}{+}{+}&{+}{+}{+}{-}&{+}{+}{-}{+}&{+}{+}{-}{-}&{+}{-}{+}{+}&{+}{-}{+}{-}&{+}{-}{-}{+}&{+}{-}{-}{-}\\\hline
\beta_{18}^{-1}(v)&7&20&\infty&14&4&19&8&17
\end{array}
$$
$$
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
v&{-}{+}{+}{+}&{-}{+}{+}{-}&{-}{+}{-}{+}&{-}{+}{-}{-}&{-}{-}{+}{+}&{-}{-}{+}{-}&{-}{-}{-}{+}&{-}{-}{-}{-}\\\hline
\beta_{18}^{-1}(v)&21&3&16&11&22&10&9&18
\end{array}
$$
Each generator of $K_{18}$, transported by $\beta_{18}$, maps the $24$ spanning words of $\mathcal G_{24}$ to codewords, so $K_{18}\le K_{\beta_{18}}$, and maximality gives $K_{\beta_{18}}=K_{18}$.

Item 5. The first statement is (U.71a.1) for $g=\iota$. The exponents $1,5,7,11$ of $F_4$ are odd, so $c^6=-I=\iota$, and $g_6^3(x)=-\omega^3x\omega^3=-x$. The classes of item 4 that contain $\iota$ lie in conjugates of $\langle c\rangle$ or $\langle g_6\rangle$, because the three involutions of $K_{18}$ are the maps $-s$ for the reflections $s$ in $e_2-e_3$, $e_2-e_4$, $e_3-e_4$. The fixed-point-free involutions of $M_{24}$ form one conjugacy class (Conway and Sloane 1999), so the remaining statements follow from one representative $z=\beta^{-1}\iota\beta$: it preserves exactly $15$ octads, its fixed subcode has dimension $6$, and the images of the fixed codewords on the twelve $z$-orbits are pairwise orthogonal with the stated weight distribution. A six-dimensional self-orthogonal code of length $12$ is self-dual. ∎

<a id="proposition-u71b-grassmannian-fixed-planes-and-equivariant-line-marking"></a>**Proposition U.71b (Grassmannian Fixed Planes and Equivariant Line Marking).** Let $M_{24}$ act on $\mathbb C^\Omega$ and $W(F_4)$ on $\mathbb C^{V_{24}}$ by permuting coordinates, and write $E_\lambda:=\ker(L_W-\lambda)$.

1. For $2\le r\le22$ no $r$-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^\Omega$ is $M_{24}$-invariant; in particular $M_{24}$ fixes no point of $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(12,\mathbb C^\Omega)$.

2. $W(F_4)$ fixes exactly two points of $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(12,\mathbb C^{V_{24}})$: the antipodally even plane $E_\pm(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{line}})=E_0\oplus E_8\oplus E_{24}$ and the odd plane $E_3\oplus E_{15}$.

3. With the normalized inner products of Definition U.32 and Theorem U.13b, the $W(F_4)$-equivariant isometries $J:\mathcal S_{\mathrm{line}}\to\mathbb C^{V_{24}}$ are exactly
$$
J=E_\pm\bigl(e^{i\theta_8}P_8+e^{i\theta_{-4}}P_{-4}+e^{i\theta_0}P_0\bigr),
\qquad \theta_8,\theta_{-4},\theta_0\in\mathbb R ,
\tag{U.71b.1}
$$
with $P_8,P_{-4},P_0$ as in Theorem U.44d.

Consequently every complex reference twelve-plane placed on the code coordinates has a proper stabilizer in $M_{24}$, while on the $24$-cell side the equivariant line marking is $E_\pm$ up to the three phases of (U.71b.1).

*Proof.* Item 1. $M_{24}$ is $5$-transitive on $\Omega$ (Conway and Sloane 1999), so it has two orbits on ordered pairs and the commutant of $\mathbb C^\Omega$ is two-dimensional. The invariant decomposition $\mathbb C^\Omega=\mathbb C\mathbf 1\oplus\mathbf 1^\perp$ therefore consists of two non-isomorphic irreducible summands, and the invariant subspaces are $0$, $\mathbb C\mathbf 1$, $\mathbf 1^\perp$ and $\mathbb C^\Omega$, of dimensions $0,1,23,24$.

Item 2. The proof of Theorem U.44d shows that $W(F_4)$ is transitive on ordered vertex pairs with each inner product. It therefore has five orbits on ordered pairs, indexed by $\langle v,w\rangle\in\{1,\frac12,0,-\frac12,-1\}$, and the commutant of $\mathbb C^{V_{24}}$ is five-dimensional. The operator $L_W$ is a combination of the corresponding relation matrices, so it commutes with $W(F_4)$, and Proposition U.13a gives five nonzero invariant eigenspaces of dimensions $1,4,9,8,2$ for $\lambda=0,3,8,15,24$. A five-dimensional commutant forces these summands to be irreducible and pairwise non-isomorphic, so the invariant subspaces are the sums of eigenspaces. The only dimension sums equal to $12$ are $1+9+2$ and $4+8$. Proposition U.13a makes $E_0$, $E_8$, $E_{24}$ antipodally even and $E_3$, $E_{15}$ odd, and $E_\pm$ is a bijection of $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{line}}$ onto the even functions.

Item 3. The identity $\frac1{24}\sum_v|f(\ell_v)|^2=\frac1{12}\sum_L|f(L)|^2$ makes $E_\pm$ an isometry. Each line adjacent to $\ell_v$ contains exactly one vertex $w$ with $\langle v,w\rangle=\frac12$, so on even functions the vertex adjacency acts as the line adjacency, and Proposition U.13a sends $\mathcal S_8$, $\mathcal S_{-4}$, $\mathcal S_0$ onto $E_0$, $E_{24}$, $E_8$. An equivariant isometry has an invariant twelve-dimensional image isomorphic to $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{line}}$, whose irreducible summands have dimensions $1,2,9$ by Theorem U.44d. The odd plane has summands of dimensions $4$ and $8$, so the image is the even plane. Then $E_\pm^{-1}J$ is a unitary of $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{line}}$ commuting with $W(F_4)$, and Schur's lemma makes it a phase on each of the three non-isomorphic summands. ∎

<a id="theorem-u71c-finite-harmonic-response-encoders-and-common-unitary-markings"></a>**Theorem U.71c (Finite Harmonic-Response Encoders and Common Unitary Markings).** Fix the field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and real form of Definition U.41a, and abbreviate $S=\mathcal S_{\mathrm{line}}^{\mathbb F}$, $V=V_{24}$ and $\mathcal L=\mathcal L_{12}$. Give $S$ the normalized line inner product and $\mathbb F^V$ the normalized vertex inner product $\langle a,b\rangle=24^{-1}\sum_v\bar a(v)b(v)$. Write
$$
M_d=D_{h_d}E_\pm,\qquad A:S\to T:=(\mathbb F^V)^5,
\qquad Af=(M_1f,\ldots,M_5f),
$$
with the direct-sum inner product on $T$. This is the shared response map of (U.41a.4). For any representative $v_L$ of a line define
$$
w_L=\sum_{d=1}^5h_d(v_L)^2,\qquad Z=\{L:w_L=0\},\qquad z=|Z|.
$$
Parity makes $w_L$ independent of the representative. The normalized adjoint satisfies
$$
A^*A=\operatorname{diag}(w_L),\qquad\ker A=\mathbb F^Z.
$$
For $r=(r_d)\in T$ define
$$
b_L(r)=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{d=1}^5\sum_{v\in L}h_d(v)r_d(v)}{2w_L},&w_L>0,\\
0,&w_L=0.
\end{cases}
$$
Then $b(r)=A^+r$ is the Moore--Penrose inverse.

Let $X$ be a finite record set with independently specified responses $r_d:X\to\mathbb F^V$. Every encoder $e:X\to S$ satisfying all five equations $M_de(x)=r_d(x)$ is classified as follows. A solution exists exactly when
$$
r_d(x)(v)=h_d(v)b_{[v]}(r(x))\qquad(x\in X,\ v\in V,\ 1\le d\le5).
$$
When this test passes, all solutions are
$$
e(x)=b(r(x))+k_x,\qquad k_x\in\mathbb F^Z,
$$
with independent kernel choices. The solution space has affine dimension $|X|z$. If $z=0$, the solution is unique and is injective exactly when the response tuples separate records. If $z>0$, an injective solution exists for every passing finite response table.

*Proof.* Each column has support on its antipodal pair. Calculating the adjoint with weights $1/12$ and $1/24$ gives the displayed diagonal Gram matrix and inverse. Thus $AA^+$ is the projection onto $\operatorname{im}A$, and the finite test is precisely $r(x)=AA^+r(x)$. Every solution fiber is $A^+r(x)+\ker A$. Different response fibers cannot collide under an encoder. Within each equal-response fiber choose distinct kernel vectors when $z>0$; this is possible over either infinite field because $X$ is finite. ∎

For a finite group $K$ acting on $X$ and permuting $\mathcal L$ through $\rho$, an equivariant encoder is specified by a vector $f_x\in S^{H_x}$ for each orbit representative, where $H_x$ is its stabilizer, and $e(gx)=\rho(g)f_x$. With fixed responses the complete additional test is the finite affine system
$$
f_x\in S^{H_x},\qquad A\rho(g)f_x=r(gx)\quad(g\in K).
$$
This formulation preserves the fixed tests even when $A$ fails to intertwine the unmodified output permutation action.

**Simultaneous unitary response markings.** Let $S_U$ be the registered twelve-dimensional Hilbert source over the same field, and let $R_d:S_U\to\mathbb F^V$ be independently specified linear responses, stacked as $R:S_U\to T$. A single unitary $J_{12}:S_U\to S$ satisfies $M_dJ_{12}=R_d$ for every degree exactly when
$$
RR^*=AA^*.
$$
All such markings are
$$
J_{12}=A^+R+W P_{\ker R},
$$
where $W:\ker R\to\ker A$ is an arbitrary unitary. Thus their residual freedom is a $U(z)$ torsor over $\mathbb C$ and an $O(z)$ torsor over $\mathbb R$. The frozen tuple (U.41c.2) has $z=0$, so a compatible marking is unique whenever it exists.

*Proof.* Necessity follows from $R=AJ_{12}$. Conversely $RR^*=AA^*$ gives equal ranges and ranks. With $J_0=A^+R$,
$$
J_0J_0^*=A^+(AA^*)(A^+)^*=P_{(\ker A)^\perp}.
$$
Since $\operatorname{im}R=\operatorname{im}A$ and $A^+$ is injective there, $\ker J_0=\ker R$. Hence $J_0$ is the unitary partial isometry from $(\ker R)^\perp$ onto $(\ker A)^\perp$. Equal source dimensions give equal kernel dimensions $z$, and the displayed extensions are exactly the unitaries completing this partial isometry. ∎

On the real branch the source real form is part of the datum, and real compatibility means mapping it onto the real-valued even-lift form of Theorem U.41c. Without independently supplied $R_d$, every bare unitary $S_U\to S$ defines responses by pullback. The criterion above selects the common marking once the response tuple is fixed.

**Equivariant finite-record encoders.** For a finite group $K$ acting on a finite record set $X$ and on the twelve lines,
$$
\operatorname{Map}_K(X,\mathbb F^{\mathcal L})
\cong\bigoplus_{[x]\in X/K}(\mathbb F^{\mathcal L})^{H_x},
$$
$$
\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{Map}_K(X,\mathbb F^{\mathcal L})
=\sum_{[x]\in X/K}|H_x\backslash\mathcal L|
=\frac1{|K|}\sum_{g\in K}|X^g|\,|\mathcal L^g|.
$$
For $H\le K$ define its line-orbit closure
$$
\overline H_{\mathcal L}
=\{g\in K:g\text{ preserves each }H\text{-orbit in }\mathcal L\text{ setwise}\}.
$$
The orbit $K/H$ admits an injective equivariant encoder exactly when $H=\overline H_{\mathcal L}$. The entire finite record set admits one exactly when this holds for every orbit stabilizer. These statements cover arbitrary functions on records, including nonlinear functions of codewords.

*Proof.* An equivariant function is determined by its value at each orbit representative, and that value is required to be fixed by its stabilizer. Fixed vectors are functions constant on stabilizer line-orbits, giving the first dimension formula. Equivariant functions are also scalar invariant functions on $X\times\mathcal L$; Burnside's count of diagonal orbits gives the second formula. Every $H$-fixed vector is fixed by $\overline H_{\mathcal L}$. Conversely, assigning distinct real values to the distinct $H$-orbits produces a vector with stabilizer exactly $\overline H_{\mathcal L}$. This proves the single-orbit criterion. For finitely many source orbits, choose disjoint coordinate-value ranges for their chosen vectors, so their target orbits cannot meet. ∎

**Encoder census on the maximal marking.** For the QR Golay code $\mathcal G_{24}$ and marking $\beta_{18}$ in Theorem U.71a, the group $K_{18}$ has $252$ codeword orbits, and
$$
\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Map}_{K_{18}}(\mathcal G_{24},\mathbb C^{\mathcal L})=2816.
$$
The registered real form has real dimension $2816$. Exactly ten codeword orbits containing $56$ words fail the injective-orbit criterion, so every equivariant encoder of the full code identifies distinct records. The complete stabilizer census is

| Codeword orbits | Orbit size | Stabilizer order | Stabilizer line-orbits | Line-orbit closure order |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | 18 | 2 | 18 |
| 213 | 18 | 1 | 12 | 1 |
| 2 | 3 | 6 | 6 | 6 |
| 9 | 6 | 3 | 6 | 6 |
| 5 | 6 | 3 | 4 | 3 |
| 18 | 9 | 2 | 9 | 2 |
| 1 | 2 | 9 | 2 | 18 |
| 2 | 3 | 6 | 3 | 6 |

*Proof.* Use the binary span of $\mathbf1_\Omega$ and $\mathbf1_{(N_{23}+s)\cup\{\infty\}}$ from Theorem U.71a, with $\infty$ represented by $23$. Generate all codewords by starting with $C_0=\{0\}$ and replacing $C_j$ by $C_j\cup(C_j+g_j)$ for each of its 24 spanning words. Generate $K_{18}$ by closure under $a(q)=\omega q$, $b(q)=q\omega$ and $\tau$, and transport these permutations by $\beta_{18}$. For each least unvisited word $c$, form the full orbit, its stabilizer $H_c$, the partition $\{H_cL:L\in\mathcal L\}$, and its setwise stabilizer inside all 18 group elements. The following fixed-space calculation gives the displayed census in doubled quaternion coordinates.

Write the doubled Hurwitz coordinates in the order
$$
2e_0,-2e_0,2e_1,-2e_1,2e_2,-2e_2,2e_3,-2e_3,
\quad (\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_3),
$$
where the sixteen sign vectors are in lexicographic order with $+1$ preceding $-1$. Pair each vector with its negative. The coordinate marking is
$$
\beta=(0,2,1,15,12,13,5,6,7,20,23,14,4,19,8,17,21,3,16,11,22,10,9,18).
$$
For doubled quaternions $u=(u_0,\mathbf u)$ and $v=(v_0,\mathbf v)$ the product is
$$
u\star v=\frac12(u_0v_0-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v,
 u_0\mathbf v+v_0\mathbf u+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v).
$$
Use $w=(-1,1,1,1)$, $a(v)=w\star v$, $b(v)=v\star w$ and
$\tau(v)=(-v_0,-v_1,-v_3,-v_2)$. Direct substitution gives
$$
a^3=b^3=\tau^2=1,\quad ab=ba,\quad \tau a\tau=b,\quad\tau b\tau=a.
$$
Thus every group element has the unique form
$g_{i,j,e}=a^ib^j\tau^e$, $i,j\in\mathbb F_3$, $e\in\{0,1\}$, with product
$$
g_{i,j,e}g_{r,s,f}=g_{(i,j)+s_e(r,s),\,e+f},\qquad
s_0(r,s)=(r,s),\quad s_1(r,s)=(s,r),
$$
where the first pair is reduced modulo three and the last coordinate modulo two. This explicitly gives all eighteen permutations.

For the binary code use
$$
N_{23}=\{5,7,10,11,14,15,17,19,20,21,22\},\quad
u_\infty=\mathbf1_\Omega,\quad
u_s=\mathbf1_{(N_{23}+s)\cup\{23\}},\quad0\le s<23.
$$
Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb F_2$ on these twenty-four vectors has rank twelve. It also gives rank twelve after the images under each of $a,b,\tau$ are adjoined, proving that the whole group preserves the code. Choose any resulting basis $b_1,\ldots,b_{12}$. For a subgroup $H$, form the binary matrix whose rows are all coordinate equations of
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{12}z_j(hb_j-b_j)=0\quad(h\in H).
$$
If its rank is $r_H$, then $d_H=12-r_H$ and exactly $2^{d_H}$ codewords are fixed by $H$. These ranks are calculated by scanning columns in order, selecting a nonzero pivot, and adding its row to every other row with a one in that column; each pivot lowers the remaining row and column counts. This is finite arithmetic on the displayed generators.

Let $A_H$ count words whose stabilizer is exactly $H$. Counting each fixed word by its exact stabilizer gives the descending recurrence
$$
 A_H=2^{d_H}-\sum_{K\supsetneq H}A_K.
$$
Let $b_H$ be the number of $H$-orbits on the twelve antipodal lines and let $k_H$ be the order of their pointwise setwise stabilizer: a permutation belongs to this stabilizer precisely when it preserves each of those line-orbits as a set. The complete fixed-space calculation is:

| Subgroup | $\vert H\vert$ | $d_H$ | $A_H$ | $b_H$ | $k_H$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| $\langle 1\rangle$ | $1$ | $12$ | $3834$ | $12$ | $1$ |
| $\langle g_{0,0,1}\rangle$ | $2$ | $6$ | $54$ | $9$ | $2$ |
| $\langle g_{1,2,1}\rangle$ | $2$ | $6$ | $54$ | $9$ | $2$ |
| $\langle g_{2,1,1}\rangle$ | $2$ | $6$ | $54$ | $9$ | $2$ |
| $\langle g_{0,1,0}\rangle$ | $3$ | $4$ | $12$ | $4$ | $3$ |
| $\langle g_{1,0,0}\rangle$ | $3$ | $4$ | $12$ | $4$ | $3$ |
| $\langle g_{1,1,0}\rangle$ | $3$ | $4$ | $6$ | $4$ | $3$ |
| $\langle g_{1,2,0}\rangle$ | $3$ | $6$ | $54$ | $6$ | $6$ |
| $\langle g_{0,0,1},g_{1,1,0}\rangle$ | $6$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $6$ |
| $\langle g_{0,0,1},g_{1,2,0}\rangle$ | $6$ | $3$ | $6$ | $6$ | $6$ |
| $\langle g_{0,1,1}\rangle$ | $6$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $6$ |
| $\langle g_{0,2,1}\rangle$ | $6$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $6$ |
| $\langle g_{0,1,0},g_{1,0,0}\rangle$ | $9$ | $2$ | $2$ | $2$ | $18$ |
| $\langle g_{0,0,1},g_{0,1,0}\rangle$ | $18$ | $1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $18$ |

The subgroup list is exhaustive. Subgroups of $\langle a,b\rangle\cong\mathbb F_3^2$ are its zero subspace, four lines and the whole plane. For a subgroup meeting the other coset, its intersection with that plane is invariant under coordinate interchange. The possibilities are zero, the diagonal line, the antidiagonal line and the plane. The square of $g_{i,j,1}$ is $g_{i+j,i+j,0}$. This gives respectively the three order-two groups, the three diagonal order-six groups, the one antidiagonal order-six group and the whole group listed above.

A word with stabilizer $H$ has orbit size $18/|H|$. Hence the number of code orbits with any specified values $(r,h,b,k)$ is exactly
$$
\frac1r\sum_{\substack{H:\ |H|=h,\ 18/h=r\\ b_H=b,\ k_H=k}}A_H.
$$
Substitution of the fourteen displayed rows gives the eight census rows above. This supplies both their values and their exhaustiveness. The antipodal equality constraints on the twelve binary basis coefficients have rank five, so exactly $2^{12-5}=128$ codewords are constant on antipodal pairs. The octad used in the construction also has the explicit membership identity
$$
\mathbf1_{\{0,1,2,3,4,7,10,12\}}
=\nu_\infty+\nu_0+\nu_3+\nu_4+\nu_6+\nu_8.
$$

The fixed-space recurrence counts every word by one exact stabilizer, and the orbit-size division counts each orbit once. As an independent sum, the group element counts by (order, fixed codewords, fixed lines) are $(1,4096,12)$ once, $(2,64,6)$ three times, $(3,64,3)$ twice, $(3,16,0)$ six times and $(6,4,0)$ six times. Burnside gives
$$
\frac{4096+3\cdot64+2\cdot64+6\cdot16+6\cdot4}{18}=252,
\qquad
\frac{4096\cdot12+3\cdot64\cdot6+2\cdot64\cdot3}{18}=2816.
$$
The closure criterion identifies the nine size-six orbits and the one size-two orbit as the failures. ∎

A short obstruction uses the dodecad
$$
D=\{0,1,5,8,9,10,11,12,14,18,19,21\}.
$$
With $B_s=(N_{23}+s)\cup\{\infty\}$, its indicator is
$$
\mathbf1_D=\mathbf1_\Omega+\mathbf1_{B_1}+\mathbf1_{B_2}+\mathbf1_{B_6}+\mathbf1_{B_8}+\mathbf1_{B_{10}}
$$
over $\mathbb F_2$. The explicit permutations give $aD=bD=D$ and $\tau D=\Omega\setminus D$. The subgroup $\langle a,b\rangle\cong C_3^2$ and $K_{18}$ have the same two line-orbits: the lines of $1,\omega,\omega^2$ and the other nine lines. This follows by evaluating $\omega^u q\omega^v$ for $u,v\in\{0,1,2\}$ and then $\tau$ on the twelve lines. Every equivariant encoder therefore sends $D$ to a vector fixed by $\tau$, giving $e(D)=e(\Omega\setminus D)$.

On a marking with $\iota\in K_\beta$, the antipodal element acts trivially on the line carrier but fixes only $2^6$ of the $2^{12}$ codewords by Theorem U.71a, item 5. Thus equivariance also forces distinct-word identifications on those branches, including the maximal $C_{12}$ branch. Injectivity for any other specified subgroup is decided by its own line-orbit closure test.

**Rigidity of the frozen response tuple.** For the tests (U.41c.2), let $P_\pi$ act on vertex functions by $(P_\pi f)(v)=f(\pi^{-1}v)$ for an arbitrary vertex permutation $\pi$. If a single unitary $U:S\to S$ satisfies
$$
P_\pi M_d=M_dU\qquad(1\le d\le5),
$$
then $\pi=\operatorname{id}$ and $U=I$. The degree-one and degree-two equations suffice.

*Proof.* Put $t(v)=\langle(1,2,4,8),v\rangle$. Its 24 distinct values are
$$
\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm8\}\cup
\{\pm\tfrac12,\pm\tfrac32,\ldots,\pm\tfrac{15}2\}.
$$
The first tests are $h_1(v)=2t(v)$ and $h_2(v)=4t(v)^2-85$, both nonzero at every vertex. In the normalized indicator basis, columns of $M_1$ have disjoint two-point supports, the antipodal pairs. A column of $M_1U$ with $k$ nonzero coefficients has support $2k$, without cancellation. Thus the intertwining equation makes $U$ monomial and $\pi$ preserve antipodal pairs. Each nonzero unitary coefficient has modulus one; comparison of real nonzero entries makes it a sign $\eta=\pm1$. On a matched pair the first equation gives $t(\pi v)=\eta t(v)$. Therefore $h_2(\pi v)=h_2(v)$, while the second equation gives $h_2(\pi v)=\eta h_2(v)$. Nonvanishing forces $\eta=1$. Distinctness of all $t(v)$ then gives $\pi v=v$ and all coefficients equal one. ∎

Literal preservation of the frozen responses fixes the three source phases of Proposition U.71b as well. Covariant transport has a different exact identity: for any antipodal-pair-preserving $\pi$, let $Q_\pi$ be its line permutation and $h'_d=P_\pi h_d$. Then
$$
M_d(h'_d)Q_\pi=P_\pi M_d(h_d).
$$
Both sides at $v$ equal $h_d(\pi^{-1}v)f([\pi^{-1}v])$. For $\pi\in W(F_4)$, the transported test is still harmonic of the same degree. Thus simultaneous transport of tests and output rows preserves all five response maps. A code-label marking similarly transports vertex rows and pulls back the antipodal pairing.

**Raw code-response obstruction and exact alternatives.** Fix any marking $\beta:\Omega\to V_{24}$ and a harmonic tuple containing a test nonzero at every vertex, as does (U.41c.2). Regard codewords as ordinary zero-one coordinate vectors and prescribe their raw responses by
$$
r_d^\beta(c)=D_{h_d}P_\beta c.
$$
There is no function $e:\mathcal G_{24}\to\mathbb C^{\mathcal L}$ with $M_de(c)=r_d^\beta(c)$ for all words and degrees. The same obstruction holds for the set of all 759 octads.

*Proof.* The nonvanishing test is invertible as a diagonal vertex operator, so its equation forces $E_\pm e(c)=P_\beta c$. Every included word must therefore be constant on each antipodal pair. The octad incidence matrix has
$$
B^{\mathsf T}B=176I+77\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}
$$
by Theorem U.5. Its eigenvalues are $176$ on the 23-dimensional complement of constants and $2024$ on constants, so the real octad span is all of $\mathbb R^{24}$. It cannot fit in the twelve-dimensional even plane under any marking. Since the full code contains the octads, both assertions follow. ∎

For each marking, the maximal record set on which all raw responses factor is
$$
\mathcal G_{\mathrm{ev}}^\beta
=\{c\in\mathcal G_{24}:P_\beta c\text{ is antipodally even}\}.
$$
Its unique encoder is $e_{\mathrm{ev}}(c)(L)=(P_\beta c)(v)$ for $v\in L$. It is well defined and injective. The preceding necessary equation proves maximality. ### U.71e The Actual Line/24-Cell Common Frame and Generator Mismatch

<a id="proposition-u71e-common-frame-generator-and-covariance-compatibility"></a>**Proposition U.71e (Common-Frame Generator and Covariance Compatibility).** Use the normalized twelve-line carrier, the actual signed $24$-cell angular operator of Proposition U.13a and all phase-equivariant line isometries of Proposition U.71b. Use the 24 vertices $\pm e_i$ and $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)/2$. Let the twelve antipodal lines be the source coordinates. $$

<a id="theorem-u71g-quantitative-symmetry-defect-of-the-marked-four-coordinate-response"></a>**Theorem U.71g (Quantitative Symmetry Defect of the Marked Four-Coordinate Response).** Fix the marked extended Golay code $C=C^\perp\subset\mathbb F_2^{24}$ of Theorem U.71a, with dimension twelve, distance eight, coordinate group $G=M_{24}$ and permutation matrices $\rho(g)$. <a id="theorem-u71h-exact-marked-golay-response-moments"></a>**Theorem U.71h (Exact Marked Golay Response Moments).** One has $\mathbb EY=0$ and $\mathbb EYY^T=6I_4$. Every polynomial $f$ of total degree at most seven satisfies

If $v\notin C^\perp$, translation by a codeword $c_0$ with $v\cdot c_0=1$ negates the sum, proving zero. Distance eight permits expectation one only for empty support, just as for independent signs. Polynomial expansion proves the moment claim. Mean and covariance follow with $JJ^T=6I_4$.

At degree eight the additional nonzero characters have octad support. Eight factors have odd support of size eight only when all indices are distinct. Each octad contributes its product in all $8!$ orders; empty-support terms cancel against the independent-sign moment. ∎

**Explicit nonzero instance and finite certificate.**

Use the cyclic presentation in the finite data of Theorem 14.5.7b-a: multiply each binary polynomial $m$ of degree at most eleven by
$$
g(x)=1+x+x^5+x^6+x^7+x^9+x^{11}
$$
and append its overall parity as coordinate 23. This fixes the marking relative to the ordered roots.

For $t=(1,1,0,0)^T$, set $z_i=\sqrt2(J^Tt)_i$. The octad product census is

| Product $\prod_{i\in O}z_i$ | -4 | -2 | -1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Count | 3 | 10 | 7 | 714 | 6 | 14 | 5 |

The weighted sum is fifteen. Equation (U.71h.1) is therefore $8!\,15/16=37800$, with
$$
\mathbb E(t^TY)^8=1597272,\qquad
\mathbb E(t^TY_{\rm iid})^8=1559472.
$$
The following exhaustive integer certificate checks every one of the $2^{12}$ messages and both moments. The shifted generators before parity extension are independent because their leading degrees are distinct, and appending parity preserves that independence. The generated set is linear; its verified weights are all multiples of four, so the binary polarization identity makes every pair of codewords orthogonal. Dimension twelve then implies self-duality. Thus the certificate establishes the required code parameters as well as the numerical moment values for this marking.

~~~python
from collections import Counter
from itertools import combinations, product
from functools import reduce

g = sum(1 << i for i in (0, 1, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11))
code = []
for m in range(4096):
    w = 0
    for j in range(12):
        if (m >> j) & 1:
            w ^= g << j
    code.append(w | ((w.bit_count() % 2) << 23))
assert len(set(code)) == 4096
assert Counter(w.bit_count() for w in code) == {
    0: 1, 8: 759, 12: 2576, 16: 759, 24: 1}
rows = []
for i, j in combinations(range(4), 2):
    for a, b in product((-1, 1), repeat=2):
        r = [0] * 4
        r[i], r[j] = a, b
        rows.append(r)
z = [r[0] + r[1] for r in rows]
census = Counter(
    reduce(lambda a, i: a*z[i],
           (i for i in range(24) if (w >> i) & 1), 1)
    for w in code if w.bit_count() == 8)
assert census == {-4: 3, -2: 10, -1: 7, 0: 714,
                  1: 6, 2: 14, 4: 5}
coded_sum = sum(
    sum((1 - 2*((w >> i) & 1))*z[i]
        for i in range(24))**8 for w in code)
assert coded_sum == 4096 * 16 * 1597272
counts = Counter({0: 1})
for v in z:
    nxt = Counter()
    for a, n in counts.items():
        nxt[a + v] += n
        nxt[a - v] += n
    counts = nxt
assert sum(a**8*n for a, n in counts.items()) == (
    (1 << 24) * 16 * 1559472)
~~~

\qquad (\lambda>0),
$$
so that the weighted dilations
$$
(T_\rho\phi)(x):=\rho^{-1}\phi(x/\rho)
$$
preserve the Definition U.4 action;
3. the action is twice differentiable on a declared translation- and dilation-invariant field domain, the translated and scaled critical families are differentiable there, and their tangents belong to the domain of the declared self-adjoint Hessian. Differentiation of the critical-point equation is valid in the corresponding dual space. In particular, the translation and weighted-conformal tangents have finite norm in the chosen fluctuation Hilbert space.

Then:

(a) $T_\rho\phi^*$ is again an exact critical point of $S_{\mathrm{cont}}$ for every $\rho>0$;

(b) the weighted conformal tangent
$$
s_{\mathrm{conf}}(x):=\frac{d}{d\ln\rho}\Big[\rho^{-1}\phi^*(x/\rho)\Big]_{\rho=1}
=-\phi^*(x)-x^\mu\partial_\mu\phi^*(x)
$$
lies in the Hessian kernel;

(c) $s_{\mathrm{conf}}$ is nonzero and linearly independent of the four translational zero modes of Theorem U.8.

Consequently the translation plus weighted-conformal orbit is a five-dimensional exact collective-coordinate branch through $\phi^*$. Relative to the independent $288$-direction Appendix-U reference carrier, the associated arithmetic comparison index is
$$
\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{288-5}{2}=141.5.
$$
It becomes a saddle exponent only on a five-mode carrier/intertwining certificate and the exact exponent-calibration certificate $\mathfrak C_{U,\mathrm{act}}$ of Proposition U.14.
This does not contradict Theorem U.8c, which concerns the distinct pure-coordinate tangent $s_{\mathrm{coord}}(x)=x^\mu\partial_\mu\phi^*(x)$.

*Proof.* Let $y=x/\rho$. Then
$$
(T_\rho\phi)(x)=\rho^{-1}\phi(y),
\qquad
\partial_\mu(T_\rho\phi)(x)=\rho^{-2}(\partial_\mu\phi)(y).
$$
Because $D=4$, the kinetic term is invariant:
$$
\int_{\mathbb R^4}\frac12|\nabla T_\rho\phi|^2\,d^4x
=
\int_{\mathbb R^4}\frac12|\nabla\phi|^2\,d^4y.
$$
By quartic homogeneity,
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}(T_\rho\phi(x))
=
V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho^{-1}\phi(y))
=
\rho^{-4}V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\phi(y)),
$$
so after the change of variables $d^4x=\rho^4\,d^4y$, the potential term is also invariant. Hence
$$
S_{\mathrm{cont}}[T_\rho\phi]=S_{\mathrm{cont}}[\phi]
\qquad
\text{for all }\phi,\rho>0.
$$
Since $T_\rho$ is an invertible smooth action on field space, critical points are carried to critical points, proving (a).

Differentiate the exact critical family $\rho\mapsto T_\rho\phi^*$ at $\rho=1$. The derivative is $s_{\mathrm{conf}}$, so differentiating the Euler-Lagrange equation along that family yields
$$
D^2S_{\mathrm{cont}}(\phi^*)[s_{\mathrm{conf}},\eta]=0
\qquad
\text{for all test directions }\eta,
$$
proving (b).

For (c), the translation zero modes are $t_\mu=-\partial_\mu\phi^*$. Because $\phi^*$ is $O(4)$-symmetric, each $t_\mu$ transforms in the vector representation, while $s_{\mathrm{conf}}=-\varphi(r)-r\varphi'(r)$ is an $O(4)$ scalar. Under any $O(4)$-invariant inner product, scalar and vector isotypic components are orthogonal. If $s_{\mathrm{conf}}=0$, then $r\varphi'(r)=-\varphi(r)$, so $\varphi(r)=c/r$; finite action then forces $c=0$, contradicting non-triviality. Hence $s_{\mathrm{conf}}\neq0$ and cannot lie in the translation span. Theorem U.3 gives $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_{S_U}\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(12,24)=288$. Subtracting the five continuum collective coordinates gives the arithmetic comparison index $(288-5)/2=141.5$. A five-mode analogue of $\mathfrak C_{U,\mathrm{mark}}$ is still required to intertwine these continuum directions with that independent carrier, and the exact exponent-calibration certificate $\mathfrak C_{U,\mathrm{act}}$ of Proposition U.14 is still required before the index can enter a saddle weight. The distinction from Theorem U.8c follows because $s_{\mathrm{conf}}=-\phi^*-s_{\mathrm{coord}}$ is not the pure-coordinate tangent. ∎

<a id="theorem-u73a-quartic-homogeneity-refuted-on-the-theorem-level-false-vacuum-branch"></a>**Theorem U.73a (Quartic Homogeneity Refuted on the Theorem-Level False-Vacuum Branch).** Work under the hypotheses of Theorem U.13b, and let
$$
\phi^*(x)=\varphi(|x|)
$$
be the associated non-trivial finite-action $O(4)$-symmetric one-bounce saddle. Then there is no interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ containing $0$ and the nonzero values attained by $\varphi$ on which
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda\phi)=\lambda^4V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\phi)
$$
holds for all $\phi\in I$ and all $\lambda>0$ with $\lambda\phi\in I$. In particular, the quartic-homogeneity hypothesis of Proposition U.73 does not hold on the theorem-level false-vacuum bounce branch.

*Proof.* Theorem U.13b gives
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}\in C^3(\mathbb R),
\qquad
V_{\mathrm{eff}}(0)=V_{\mathrm{eff}}'(0)=0,
\qquad
V_{\mathrm{eff}}''(0)>0,
$$
and provides a non-trivial one-bounce saddle $\phi^*(x)=\varphi(|x|)$ with
$$
\lim_{r\to\infty}\varphi(r)=0,
\qquad
\varphi'(r)<0\ \,(r>0).
$$
Because the bounce is non-trivial, there exists a nonzero value $a$ attained by $\varphi$. Assume, for contradiction, that quartic homogeneity holds on an interval containing $0$ and $a$. Then for all sufficiently small $t>0$,
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}(ta)=t^4V_{\mathrm{eff}}(a).
$$
But Taylor expansion at $0$ gives
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}(ta)=\frac12V_{\mathrm{eff}}''(0)a^2t^2+o(t^2)
\qquad (t\to0^+).
$$
Dividing by $t^2$ and letting $t\to0^+$ yields
$$
\frac12V_{\mathrm{eff}}''(0)a^2=0,
$$
contradicting $a\neq0$ and $V_{\mathrm{eff}}''(0)>0$. Therefore quartic homogeneity is impossible on this branch. ∎

<a id="corollary-u73b-four-mode-hessian-nullity-closure-and-reference-index-boundary"></a>**Corollary U.73b (Four-Mode Hessian-Nullity Closure and Reference-Index Boundary).** On the false-vacuum spectral branch of Theorem U.13b, Proposition U.73 cannot supply an unconditional fifth zero mode. The theorem-level conclusion is exactly four translation zero modes of the radially continuous, sampled-angular Hessian. On the independently registered $288$-direction Grassmannian ledger, this gives only the arithmetic reference index
$$
\kappa_{\mathrm{idx}}=\frac{288-4}{2}=142.
$$
Promoting that index to a saddle exponent requires the marking certificate $\mathfrak C_{U,\mathrm{mark}}$ of Convention U.14a and its exact exponent-calibration certificate $\mathfrak C_{U,\mathrm{act}}$. A numerical weight additionally requires $\mathfrak F_U^{(4)}$, and a cosmological constant additionally requires $\mathfrak R_\Lambda^{(4)}$.

*Proof.* Proposition U.73 requires quartic homogeneity, which Theorem U.73a refutes on this false-vacuum branch. Theorem U.13b fixes the four-mode nullity in its declared Hessian space. Convention U.14a states the independent carrier and action gates needed for exponent transport, and Definitions U.73e and U.73e.6 state the further weight and Einstein-realization gates. ∎

The domain is the same radially continuous, sampled-angular Hessian, boundary conditions, false-vacuum spectral hypotheses, and nontrivial bounce as Theorem U.13b. Equivalence permits orthogonal changes of the four translation basis vectors and registered vertex reorderings but not a change of Hessian domain or potential branch. The audit uses the exact nullity theorem and the two symbolic degrees $(2,4)$, with no cutoff, regulator, target query, or empirical datum. A fifth linearly independent kernel vector for that same operator falsifies the conclusion; setting $V_{\mathrm{eff}}''(0)=0$ instead invalidates applicability and opens a different action class. The nontrivial bounce and its four translation modes supply nonvacuity.

This obstruction settles the current false-vacuum branch only. It does not classify other critical scale families or admissible conformal actions, including an explicitly massless or otherwise altered action, and no carrier, action, determinant, or cosmological realization follows from it.

<a id="theorem-u73b2-canonical-homogeneous-scale-invariance-classification"></a>**Theorem U.73b.2 (Canonical Homogeneous Scale-Invariance Classification).** Let $D>2$, let the finitely many distinct exponents satisfy $p_j>0$, and let $\lambda_j\ne0$ after equal powers have been collected. Consider
$$
S[\phi]
=\int_{\mathbb R^D}
\left(\frac12|\nabla\phi|^2+\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j|\phi|^{p_j}\right)d^Dx.
\tag{U.73b.2.1}
$$
Require separate finiteness of these integrals on the field domain. The domain is preserved by
$$
(T_\rho\phi)(x)=\rho^{-\alpha}\phi(x/\rho),
\qquad \rho>0,
$$
and contains every $\phi_{a,L}(x)=a\psi(x/L)$ for $a,L>0$, where $\psi$ is one specified nonnegative, nonconstant smooth compactly supported profile. In particular,
$$
K_\psi:=\frac12\int|\nabla\psi|^2>0,
\qquad
P_j:=\int|\psi|^{p_j}>0
$$
are finite. The action is invariant on this domain for every $\rho>0$ exactly when
$$
\alpha=\frac{D-2}{2},
\qquad
p_j=\frac{2D}{D-2}\quad\text{for every }j.
\tag{U.73b.2.2}
$$
On this branch, a nontrivial critical point generates an exact critical scale family when the dilation action preserves the differentiable field domain. Its dilation tangent is a formal linearized solution; it belongs to the self-adjoint Hessian kernel only when the family is differentiable in the declared fluctuation domain, the tangent has finite Hilbert norm and belongs to the Hessian domain, and differentiation of the critical-point equation is valid there. In $D=4$, every nonzero potential term must therefore be quartic; a mass term or any other nonquartic homogeneous term excludes this canonical scale-symmetry mechanism.

*Proof.* A change of variables gives
$$
S[T_\rho\phi]
=\rho^{D-2-2\alpha}K[\phi]
+\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j\rho^{D-\alpha p_j}P_j[\phi],
$$
where $K[\phi]=\frac12\int|\nabla\phi|^2$ and $P_j[\phi]=\int|\phi|^{p_j}$. For an admitted $\phi_{a,L}$, invariance therefore implies
$$
0=a^2L^{D-2}K_\psi(\rho^{D-2-2\alpha}-1)
+L^D\sum_j\lambda_j a^{p_j}P_j(\rho^{D-\alpha p_j}-1)
$$
for every $a,L,\rho>0$. Divide by $L^{D-2}$ and vary $L$. The constant and $L^2$ coefficients must separately vanish. Since $a^2K_\psi>0$, the first coefficient gives $D-2-2\alpha=0$. For each $\rho$, the second gives a finite linear combination of the distinct functions $a^{p_j}$ that vanishes for all $a>0$. These functions are independent: order the exponents, divide by the largest power, let $a\to\infty$ to remove its coefficient, and repeat. Since $\lambda_jP_j\ne0$, each $\rho^{D-\alpha p_j}-1$ vanishes for every $\rho>0$. Thus $D-\alpha p_j=0$. Solving gives (U.73b.2.2). Conversely, those exponents make every displayed scaling factor one for every field with the stated finite integrals, proving invariance. An invertible differentiable symmetry of the field domain maps critical points to critical points. Differentiating that family gives the linearized equation; the declared fluctuation-domain and tangent-normalizability conditions place its solution in the self-adjoint Hessian kernel. Setting $D=4$ gives $\alpha=1$ and $p_j=4$. ∎

The theorem exhausts canonical kinetic actions with finite sums of homogeneous local potential terms. Higher-derivative conformal actions, nonlocal actions, boundary-anomalous domains, and a PU carrier realization are outside this classified action family.

<a id="theorem-u73b2a-local-potential-dilation-classification-and-the-four-dimensional-hilbert-space-obstruction"></a>**Theorem U.73b.2a (Local-Potential Dilation Classification and the Four-Dimensional Hilbert-Space Obstruction).** Let $V\in C^2$ on a neighborhood of $[0,A]$, with $V(0)=V'(0)=0$. Let $\phi_*(x)=h(|x|)$ be a positive $C^3$ solution of
$$
-\Delta\phi_*+V'(\phi_*)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb R^4,
$$
with $h(0)=A>0$, $h'(0)=0$, $0<h(r)\le A$, $h(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$, and
$$
0<\int_0^\infty r^3h'(r)^2\,dr<\infty,\qquad
\int_0^\infty r^3|V(h(r))|\,dr<\infty.
$$
For the canonical scalar action, take the Hessian $L=-\Delta+V''(\phi_*)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^4)$ with domain $H^2(\mathbb R^4)$. The multiplier is bounded, so this is the self-adjoint bounded perturbation of the free Laplacian. Put $v_{u,\tau}=u\phi_*-\tau x\cdot\nabla\phi_*$. Then:

1. For every $(u,\tau)$, its pointwise linearized residual is
$$
Lv_{u,\tau}=u\phi_*V''(\phi_*)+(2\tau-u)V'(\phi_*).
$$
A nonzero amplitude--dilation tangent solves the linearized equation exactly when
$$
V(q)=-\frac g4q^4\quad(0\le q\le A),\qquad
h(r)=\frac{A}{1+gA^2r^2/8},\qquad
u=-\tau\ne0
$$
for some $g>0$. Thus this criterion uses the potential on the attained field interval, rather than global homogeneity of the action.

2. In that case the formal dilation tangent $s=-\phi_*-x\cdot\nabla\phi_*$ satisfies
$$
s(r)=\frac{A(cr^2-1)}{(1+cr^2)^2},\qquad c=\frac{gA^2}{8}>0,
\qquad\lim_{r\to\infty}r^2s(r)=\frac A c.
$$
Consequently $s\notin L^2(\mathbb R^4)$. For every potential and profile in the stated class, the full self-adjoint Hessian has no nonzero zero mode in the amplitude--dilation tangent space. The conclusion concerns the amplitude--dilation span; translation and other shape zero modes retain their separate spectral conditions.

3. For a running parametrization $V(q)=q^4b(\log(q/\mu))$ on $0<q\le A$, with $\mu>0$ and $b\in C^2$, the residual of $s$ is
$$
Ls=-\phi_*^3\left(b''+4b'\right)\!\left(\log(\phi_*/\mu)\right).
$$
Vanishing on the attained interval forces $b$ to be constant there, after imposing $V(0)=0$. Nonconstant running on that interval therefore removes even the formal dilation solution; the constant negative-quartic branch retains the nonnormalizable solution of item 2.

*Proof.* Differentiating the Euler equation gives $L\partial_i\phi_*=0$. The product rule gives
$$
L(x\cdot\nabla\phi_*)=-2\Delta\phi_*=-2V'(\phi_*),\qquad
L\phi_*=\phi_*V''(\phi_*)-V'(\phi_*),
$$
which proves the residual identity. The tangent map is injective: if $u h-\tau rh'=0$ and $\tau=0$, then $u=0$; if $\tau\ne0$, its solutions on $r>0$ are $h(r)=Cr^{u/\tau}$, incompatible with $h(0)=A>0$ and $h(\infty)=0$.

Suppose a nonzero tangent has zero residual. The image of $h$ contains every value in $(0,A]$ by continuity. If $u=0$, then $\tau\ne0$ and $V'$ vanishes on that interval. The radial equation $(r^3h')'=r^3V'(h)$ and regularity at zero would give $h'=0$, a contradiction. Thus $u\ne0$. With $F=V'$ and $\gamma=1-2\tau/u$, the residual equation becomes $qF'(q)=\gamma F(q)$ for every $0<q\le A$. Hence $F(q)=Cq^\gamma$ on that interval. The coefficient $C$ is nonzero, since the zero coefficient again gives a constant profile. The conditions $F(0)=0$ and continuity of $F'$ at zero require $\gamma\ge1$: $\gamma\le0$ violates $F(0)=0$, and $0<\gamma<1$ makes $F'$ unbounded. Write $p=\gamma+1\ge2$. Integration using $V(0)=0$ gives $V(q)=Cq^p/p$. If $C>0$, integration of $(r^3h')'=Cr^3h^{p-1}$ from zero makes $h'>0$, contradicting its decay. Therefore $C=-g$ for some $g>0$.

Set
$$
G=\int_0^\infty r^3h'^2\,dr,\qquad P=\int_0^\infty r^3h^p\,dr.
$$
Both are finite, with $G,P>0$. The identity $h(r)=-\int_r^\infty h'(t)dt$ and weighted Cauchy--Schwarz give
$$
r^2h(r)^2\le\frac12\int_r^\infty t^3h'(t)^2dt\longrightarrow0.
$$
Since $\int_1^\infty r^3(h'^2+h^p)dr<\infty$, there is a sequence $R_n\to\infty$ with $R_n^4(h'(R_n)^2+h(R_n)^p)\to0$; otherwise the integral would dominate a positive multiple of $\int dr/r$. Along that sequence, $R_n^3h(R_n)h'(R_n)\to0$ by the preceding bound. Multiply $h''+3h'/r+gh^{p-1}=0$ first by $r^3h$ and then by $r^4h'$, integrate from zero to $R_n$, and pass to the limit. The boundary terms at zero vanish by regularity, while those at $R_n$ vanish by construction. The two identities are
$$
G=gP,\qquad G=\frac{4g}{p}P.
$$
For completeness, the second integration uses
$$
\left[\frac12r^4h'^2+\frac gp r^4h^p\right]_0^{R_n}
+\int_0^{R_n}r^3h'^2dr-\frac{4g}{p}\int_0^{R_n}r^3h^pdr=0.
$$
Since $gP>0$, $p=4$. Thus $\gamma=3$, $\tau=-u$ and $V(q)=-gq^4/4$ on the attained interval.

Direct substitution shows that $h_0(r)=A/(1+gA^2r^2/8)$ solves this radial equation with the required initial data. Regular radial solutions with that initial value are unique. Indeed they satisfy
$$
h(r)=A-g\int_0^r t^{-3}\int_0^t s^3h(s)^3\,ds\,dt.
$$
On a sufficiently small interval where two solutions are bounded, the cubic is Lipschitz with some constant $M$, and their sup-norm difference is at most $gMr^2/8$ times itself. Choosing $r$ so this factor is less than one proves equality there. Ordinary differential-equation uniqueness for positive $r$ extends equality over their common domain. Hence the given profile is $h_0$. Conversely this potential/profile pair and $u=-\tau$ make the displayed residual zero. Differentiating the rational profile gives item 2. The positive limit $r^2s(r)=A/c+o(1)$ makes its radial squared norm dominate a positive multiple of $\int_R^\infty dr/r$. Any nonzero tangent in the operator kernel would first solve the same pointwise equation, hence be such a multiple of $s$; it therefore fails the required $L^2$ membership.

Finally, differentiating $V(q)=q^4b(\log(q/\mu))$ twice yields $3V'(q)-qV''(q)=-q^3(b''+4b')$. The complete solution of $b''+4b'=0$ on $(-\infty,\log(A/\mu)]$ is $b(t)=b_0+b_1e^{-4t}$. Thus $V(q)=b_0q^4+b_1\mu^4$. Continuity at zero and $V(0)=0$ give $b_1=0$, proving item 3. ∎

<a id="proposition-u73b2b-fixed-ball-dirichlet-and-neumann-dilation-domain-obstructions"></a>**Proposition U.73b.2b (Fixed-Ball Dirichlet and Neumann Dilation-Domain Obstructions).** Let a nonconstant regular radial profile $h$ solve $h''+3h'/r=V'(h)$ on a four-dimensional ball of radius $R>0$, with $V\in C^2$ near its range. For the canonical Hessian with homogeneous Dirichlet or homogeneous Neumann boundary condition, every amplitude--dilation tangent $v=u h-\tau rh'$ with $\tau\ne0$ fails the operator boundary condition. In the Dirichlet case assume $h(R)=0$ and $V'(0)=0$; in the Neumann case assume $h'(R)=0$.

*Proof.* For Dirichlet data, $v(R)=-\tau R h'(R)$. If $h'(R)=0$, the initial data $(h(R),h'(R))=(0,0)$ for the regular radial equation near $R$ have the constant-zero solution; local uniqueness and continuation to every positive radius force $h$ to be constant, a contradiction. Hence $v(R)\ne0$. For Neumann data,
$$
v'(R)=-\tau R h''(R)=-\tau R V'(h(R)).
$$
If $V'(h(R))=0$, the constant function with value $h(R)$ solves the same radial initial-value problem at $R$, and the same uniqueness argument forces $h$ to be constant. Thus $v'(R)\ne0$. These nonzero traces exclude $v$ from the respective self-adjoint Hessian domains. ∎

<a id="theorem-u73b2c-boundary-anomalous-inverse-square-family"></a>**Theorem U.73b.2c (Boundary-Anomalous Inverse-Square Family).** Let $0<\nu<1$ and $n\ge1$, and on $L^2((0,\infty);\mathbb C^n)$ let $\mathcal T_\nu=-\frac{d^2}{dr^2}+\frac{\nu^2-1/4}{r^2}$. The expression $\mathcal T_\nu$ is homogeneous of degree $-2$ under the unitary dilations $(U_su)(r)=s^{1/2}u(sr)$: $\mathcal T_\nu U_s=s^2U_s\mathcal T_\nu$. For $u$ in the maximal domain $D_{\max}=\{u\in L^2: u,u'\ \text{locally absolutely continuous},\ \mathcal T_\nu u\in L^2\}$ the boundary values
$$
A_u=\frac1{2\nu}\lim_{r\to0}W[u,r^{1/2+\nu}],\qquad B_u=\frac1{2\nu}\lim_{r\to0}W[r^{1/2-\nu},u],\qquad W[f,g]=fg'-f'g,
$$
exist in $\mathbb C^n$; for $u=Ar^{1/2-\nu}+Br^{1/2+\nu}$ near $0$ they are $A$ and $B$. Put $C_\nu:=-2^{-2\nu}\Gamma(-\nu)/\Gamma(\nu)=\Gamma(1-\nu)/(\nu4^{\nu}\Gamma(\nu))>0$; $C_{1/2}=1$.

1. *Self-adjoint realizations.* The self-adjoint restrictions of $\mathcal T_\nu$ on $D_{\max}$ are exactly the operators $h_{E,K}$ with domain $\{u\in D_{\max}:A_u\in E,\ P_EB_u=KA_u\}$, where $E\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ is a subspace, $P_E$ its orthogonal projection and $K=K^{*}$ acts on $E$.
2. *The dilation acts on the boundary datum.* $U_s$ maps the domain of $h_{E,K}$ onto that of $h_{E,s^{2\nu}K}$, and $h_{E,s^{2\nu}K}=s^{2}U_sh_{E,K}U_s^{-1}$. The realization is dilation covariant exactly when $K=0$; for $K\ne0$ the scaling symmetry of the expression is broken by the domain, and the boundary datum runs as $K\mapsto s^{2\nu}K$.
3. *Spectrum.* Every $h_{E,K}$ has essential spectrum $[0,\infty)$ and no eigenvalue in $[0,\infty)$. Its negative eigenvalues are exactly $-(-\eta/C_\nu)^{1/\nu}$ for the negative eigenvalues $\eta$ of $K$, with the same multiplicities and eigenfunctions $\sqrt r\,K_\nu(\kappa r)\,e$, $Ke=\eta e$, $\kappa=(-\eta/C_\nu)^{1/(2\nu)}$.
4. *Hessians with a mass term.* For $\mu>0$ let $H=h_{E,K}+\mu^2$. Its essential spectrum is $[\mu^2,\infty)$, its number of negative eigenvalues is the number of eigenvalues of $K$ below $-C_\nu\mu^{2\nu}$, and
 $$\ker H=\{\sqrt r\,K_\nu(\mu r)\,e:\ e\in\ker(K+C_\nu\mu^{2\nu})\}.$$
 For $\mu=0$ the kernel is trivial. Zero modes therefore occur exactly on the boundary data with $\det(K+C_\nu\mu^{2\nu})=0$.
5. *The dilation tangent leaves the domain.* For an eigenfunction $u$ of $h_{E,K}$ the dilation tangent $Du=\frac{d}{ds}U_su|_{s=1}=(\tfrac12+r\frac{d}{dr})u$ lies in $D_{\max}$ with boundary values $((1-\nu)A_u,(1+\nu)B_u)$, so $P_EB_{Du}-KA_{Du}=2\nu KA_u=2\nu\eta A_u\neq0$. The scale direction is not an admissible fluctuation of a bound state.
6. *Variation of the boundary datum.* Along a differentiable family $K(\epsilon)$ with a simple eigenvalue $\eta(\epsilon)$, $\eta(0)=-C_\nu\mu^{2\nu}$, the corresponding eigenvalue of $H$ is $\lambda(\epsilon)=\mu^2-(-\eta(\epsilon)/C_\nu)^{1/\nu}$, with $\lambda'(0)=\mu^{2-2\nu}\eta'(0)/(\nu C_\nu)$. By item 4 the zero mode persists exactly while $K(\epsilon)$ keeps the eigenvalue $-C_\nu\mu^{2\nu}$. For $\nu=\tfrac12$, where $\mathcal T_\nu=-d^2/dr^2$ with the Robin condition $P_Eu'(0)=Ku(0)$, $\mu=1$ and $K=\operatorname{diag}(-2,-1)$, the spectrum of $H$ is $\{-3,0\}\cup[1,\infty)$; $K_{22}=-1+\epsilon$ moves the zero eigenvalue to $2\epsilon-\epsilon^2$, while $K(t)=\begin{pmatrix}-2&t\\t&-1\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalue near $-1$ has zero derivative at $t=0$, moves it to $2t^2-3t^4+O(t^6)$.

*Proof.* The scalar expression is in the limit-circle case at $0$, because both solutions $r^{1/2\pm\nu}$ of $\mathcal T_\nu u=0$ are square integrable there for $0<\nu<1$, and in the limit-point case at infinity. For $u\in D_{\max}$ and a solution $\varphi$ of $\mathcal T_\nu\varphi=0$, $W[u,\varphi]'=(\mathcal T_\nu u)\varphi$ is integrable near $0$, so the limits exist; $W[r^{1/2-\nu},r^{1/2+\nu}]=2\nu$ gives the normalization. Green's formula reads $\langle\mathcal T_\nu u,v\rangle-\langle u,\mathcal T_\nu v\rangle=-2\nu(\langle A_u,B_v\rangle-\langle B_u,A_v\rangle)$, and $u\mapsto(A_u,B_u)$ maps $D_{\max}$ onto $\mathbb C^n\oplus\mathbb C^n$ with kernel the minimal domain, so the self-adjoint restrictions correspond to the Lagrangian subspaces $\Lambda$ of this form. Let $E$ be the projection of $\Lambda$ to the $A$-coordinate. Isotropy places $\Lambda\cap(\{0\}\oplus\mathbb C^n)$ inside $\{0\}\oplus E^\perp$, and $\dim\Lambda=n$ forces equality; hence $P_EB$ is a linear function $KA$ of $A\in E$, and isotropy makes $K$ Hermitian. Conversely every pair $(E,K)$ defines a Lagrangian subspace. This is item 1; for $n=1$ it is the classical description of the self-adjoint realizations of the Bessel operator. Item 2: $U_s(Ar^{1/2-\nu}+Br^{1/2+\nu})=s^{1-\nu}Ar^{1/2-\nu}+s^{1+\nu}Br^{1/2+\nu}$, so $(A,B)\mapsto(s^{1-\nu}A,s^{1+\nu}B)$ and the condition $P_EB=KA$ becomes $P_EB=s^{2\nu}KA$; the operator identity follows from $\mathcal T_\nu U_s=s^2U_s\mathcal T_\nu$. Item 3: the deficiency indices are finite, so all realizations share the essential spectrum $[0,\infty)$ of the Friedrichs one. The solutions of $\mathcal T_\nu u=\lambda u$ that are square integrable at infinity are multiples of $\sqrt r\,K_\nu(\kappa r)$ for $\lambda=-\kappa^2<0$, and there are none for $\lambda\ge0$, where the solutions are combinations of $r^{1/2\pm\nu}$ or oscillate. From $K_\nu(z)=\tfrac12\Gamma(\nu)(z/2)^{-\nu}+\tfrac12\Gamma(-\nu)(z/2)^{\nu}+\dots$ the boundary values of $\sqrt rK_\nu(\kappa r)e$ satisfy $B=-C_\nu\kappa^{2\nu}A$ with $A$ a nonzero multiple of $e$; the boundary condition is $e\in E$ and $Ke=-C_\nu\kappa^{2\nu}e$. Item 4 is item 3 shifted by $\mu^2$. Item 5: $U_s$ applied to $\sqrt rK_\nu(\kappa r)e$ gives $s\sqrt rK_\nu(\kappa sr)e$, a smooth family in $D_{\max}$, and differentiating the boundary values of item 2 at $s=1$ gives the stated residual. Item 6 differentiates the eigenvalue formula of item 3 and uses the kernel statement of item 4; for $\nu=\tfrac12$, $C_{1/2}=1$ and $\lambda=1-\eta^2$, and the eigenvalue of $K(t)$ near $-1$ is $(-3+\sqrt{1+4t^2})/2$. ∎

For $\nu=\tfrac12$ the operator $H$ is the Hessian of the quadratic action $\frac12\int_0^\infty(|f'|^2+\mu^2|f|^2)\,dr+\frac12f(0)^*Kf(0)$ on $\{f\in H^1((0,\infty);\mathbb C^n):f(0)\in E\}$, whose variation gives the Robin condition $P_Ef'(0)=Kf(0)$. In this family the realizations are dilation covariant exactly when $K=0$, and they then have no eigenvalue; for $\mu>0$ zero modes occur exactly on the boundary data with $\det(K+C_\nu\mu^{2\nu})=0$, and no bound state has its dilation tangent in the domain. Every zero mode of the family is fixed by the boundary datum and none is generated by the scale covariance of the bulk expression.

<a id="proposition-u73b2d-fixed-ball-robin-and-dirichlet-kernel-classification"></a>**Proposition U.73b.2d (Fixed-Ball Robin and Dirichlet Kernel Classification).** Let $R>0$, let $h\in C^2([0,R])$ be nonconstant with $h'(0)=0$ and $h''+3h'/r=V'(h)$ on $(0,R]$, where $V\in C^2$ on a neighborhood of $h([0,R])$, and put $\phi_*(x)=h(|x|)$ on the closed ball $\overline B_R\subset\mathbb R^4$. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$ let $H_\beta=-\Delta+V''(\phi_*)$ on $L^2(B_R)$ with domain $\{\eta\in H^2(B_R):\partial_r\eta+\beta\eta=0\text{ on }\partial B_R\}$, and let $H_\infty$ be the same expression on $H^2(B_R)\cap H^1_0(B_R)$. When $h'(R)+\beta h(R)=0$, $H_\beta$ is the Hessian at $\phi_*$ of
$$
\int_{B_R}\Bigl(\frac12|\nabla\phi|^2+V(\phi)\Bigr)dx+\frac\beta2\int_{\partial B_R}\phi^2\,d\sigma ,
$$
and when $h(R)=0$, $H_\infty$ is the Hessian of the first integral on fields vanishing on $\partial B_R$. For each integer $\ell\ge0$ let $\eta_\ell$ be the solution of
$$
\eta''+\frac3r\eta'-\Bigl(\frac{\ell(\ell+2)}{r^2}+V''(h(r))\Bigr)\eta=0,\qquad r^{-\ell}\eta(r)\to1\quad(r\downarrow0),
\tag{U.73b.2d.1}
$$
and let $\mathcal Y_\ell$ be the space of spherical harmonics of degree $\ell$ on $S^3$, of dimension $(\ell+1)^2$. Put $\Lambda_\beta=\{\ell:\eta_\ell'(R)+\beta\eta_\ell(R)=0\}$ for $\beta\in\mathbb R$ and $\Lambda_\infty=\{\ell:\eta_\ell(R)=0\}$. Then, for every $\beta\in\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$,
$$
\ker H_\beta=\bigoplus_{\ell\in\Lambda_\beta}\bigl\{\eta_\ell(|x|)\,Y(x/|x|):Y\in\mathcal Y_\ell\bigr\},
\qquad
\dim\ker H_\beta=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda_\beta}(\ell+1)^2 .
\tag{U.73b.2d.2}
$$
Consequently:

1. A sector with $\eta_\ell(R)\ne0$ contributes for exactly one finite $\beta$, namely $\beta_\ell(R)=-\eta_\ell'(R)/\eta_\ell(R)$, and not for the Dirichlet domain; a sector with $\eta_\ell(R)=0$ contributes for the Dirichlet domain and for no finite $\beta$.
2. $h''(0)\ne0$ and $\eta_1=h'/h''(0)$. The four translation-shaped vectors $\partial_\mu\phi_*=h'(|x|)x_\mu/|x|$ lie in $\ker H_\beta$ exactly when $h''(R)+\beta h'(R)=0$ for finite $\beta$, and exactly when $h'(R)=0$ for the Dirichlet domain.
3. $\dim\ker H_\beta=5$ exactly when $\Lambda_\beta=\{0,1\}$; the kernel is then spanned by the four translation-shaped vectors and the radial vector $\eta_0(|x|)$.

*Proof.* The Robin and Dirichlet Laplacians of the ball are self-adjoint on the displayed $H^2$ domains, and $V''(\phi_*)$ is a bounded continuous radial multiplier, so each $H_\beta$ is self-adjoint. The first variation of the displayed action has boundary term $\int_{\partial B_R}(\partial_r\phi+\beta\phi)\,\delta\phi\,d\sigma$ and its second variation is $\int_{B_R}(|\nabla\eta|^2+V''(\phi_*)\eta^2)\,dx+\beta\int_{\partial B_R}\eta^2\,d\sigma$, whose operator is $H_\beta$; the Dirichlet case is the same computation on fields vanishing on the boundary.

Equation (U.73b.2d.1) has a regular singular point at $r=0$ with indicial exponents $\ell$ and $-\ell-2$ and a bounded continuous coefficient $V''(h(r))$. Variation of constants against $r^{\ell}$ and $r^{-\ell-2}$ turns it, with the normalization $r^{-\ell}\eta\to1$, into a Volterra equation with bounded kernel, which has a unique continuous solution $\eta_\ell$. Since $\eta_\ell>0$ near $0$, reduction of order gives a second solution $\eta_\ell(r)\int_r^{R}s^{-3}\eta_\ell(s)^{-2}\,ds=r^{-\ell-2}(2\ell+2)^{-1}(1+o(1))$, for which $\int_0r^3|\eta'|^2\,dr=\infty$.

Let $\eta\in\ker H_\beta$ and expand $\eta(r\omega)=\sum_{\ell,k}c_{\ell k}(r)Y_{\ell k}(\omega)$ in an orthonormal basis $\{Y_{\ell k}\}_k$ of each $\mathcal Y_\ell$. Because the multiplier is radial, each coefficient solves (U.73b.2d.1) weakly, hence classically, on $(0,R)$, and $\sum_{\ell,k}\int_0^Rr^3|c_{\ell k}'|^2\,dr\le\|\nabla\eta\|_{L^2(B_R)}^2<\infty$. Hence $c_{\ell k}=a_{\ell k}\eta_\ell$. The traces of $\eta$ and $\partial_r\eta$ on $\partial B_R$ have coefficients $a_{\ell k}\eta_\ell(R)$ and $a_{\ell k}\eta_\ell'(R)$, so the boundary condition holds exactly when $a_{\ell k}=0$ for every $\ell\notin\Lambda_\beta$. Conversely, for $\ell\in\Lambda_\beta$ and $Y\in\mathcal Y_\ell$ the function $w=\eta_\ell(|x|)Y(x/|x|)$ is bounded, lies in $H^1(B_R)$ because $|\nabla w|^2=O(r^{2\ell-2})$ near the origin, and solves $-\Delta w+V''(\phi_*)w=0$ on $B_R\setminus\{0\}$; since a point has zero capacity in four dimensions it solves the equation weakly on $B_R$, elliptic regularity places it in $H^2(B_R)$, and it satisfies the boundary condition. This proves (U.73b.2d.2).

Item 1 is immediate from the definitions. For item 2, differentiating the radial equation shows that $h'$ solves (U.73b.2d.1) with $\ell=1$; it is bounded with $h'(r)/r\to h''(0)$, hence $h'=h''(0)\eta_1$, and $h''(0)=0$ would make $h'$ vanish identically. For item 3, the dimensions $(\ell+1)^2$ are $1,4,9,16,\ldots$, and a sum over distinct $\ell$ equals $5$ only for $\{0,1\}$. ∎

The fixed ball breaks the dilation and translation invariance of the action, and (U.73b.2d.2) gives the complete kernel at every radial saddle and every homogeneous Robin or Dirichlet datum, Neumann data being $\beta=0$. A five-dimensional kernel requires the two boundary equations $0\in\Lambda_\beta$ and $1\in\Lambda_\beta$.

<a id="theorem-u73b3-bidegree-classification-of-weighted-dilation-invariance-and-the-amplitude-dilation-hessian"></a>**Theorem U.73b.3 (Bidegree Classification of Weighted-Dilation Invariance and the Amplitude--Dilation Hessian).** Let $D\ge1$ and let $\mathcal D$ be a field domain of real functions on $\mathbb R^D$ that is invariant under
$$
(\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi)(x):=e^{u}\phi(e^{-\tau}x),
\qquad (u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^2 .
$$
A functional $F$ on $\mathcal D$ has bidegree $(p,q)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ when
$$
F[\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi]=e^{pu+(D-q)\tau}F[\phi]
\qquad(\phi\in\mathcal D,\ (u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^2).
\tag{U.73b.3.1}
$$
For example, $\int|\nabla^k\phi|^2$ has bidegree $(2,2k)$, $\int\phi\,(-\Delta)^{\sigma}\phi$ has $(2,2\sigma)$, $\int|\phi|^p$ has $(p,0)$, $\int\phi^n$ with $n\in\mathbb N$ has $(n,0)$, $\int|\phi|^n|\nabla\phi|^r$ has $(n+r,r)$, and the nonlocal term $\iint|\phi(x)|^a|\phi(y)|^b|x-y|^{-\gamma}\,dx\,dy$ has $(a+b,\gamma-D)$. Let $S=\sum_{j=1}^mF_j$, where terms of equal bidegree have been combined, the bidegrees $(p_j,q_j)$ are pairwise distinct, and no $F_j$ vanishes identically on $\mathcal D$. Put $w_j:=(p_j,D-q_j)$ and $c_j(\alpha):=D-\alpha p_j-q_j$.

1. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $S$ is invariant under $T^{(\alpha)}_\rho\phi(x):=\rho^{-\alpha}\phi(x/\rho)$ for every $\rho>0$ exactly when $c_j(\alpha)=0$ for every $j$, that is, when every $w_j$ is a positive multiple of $(1,\alpha)$. A weighted-dilation symmetry therefore exists exactly when the vectors $w_j$ are pairwise proportional, and its weight $\alpha=(D-q_j)/p_j$ is then unique. With an order-$2k$ kinetic term of bidegree $(2,2k)$ this weight is $\alpha=(D-2k)/2$; a zero-derivative term of degree $p$ is then admissible exactly when $D>2k$ and $p=2D/(D-2k)$, and for $D=2k$ every term must have $q_j=D$. Kinetic terms of bidegrees $(2,2)$ and $(2,4)$ together exclude every weighted-dilation symmetry. Theorem U.73b.2 is the case of bidegrees $(2,2)$ and $(p_j,0)$.

2. Let $S$ be $C^2$ on an open field domain modeled on a real Banach space $X$, let $\phi_*\in\mathcal D$ be a critical point, and let $(u,\tau)\mapsto\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi_*$ be a $C^2$ map into that domain near $(0,0)$ with $\partial_u\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi_*|_{(0,0)}=\phi_*$ and $\partial_\tau\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi_*|_{(0,0)}=-x\cdot\nabla\phi_*$ in $X$. With $f_j:=F_j[\phi_*]$,
$$
\sum_{j=1}^mf_jw_j=0,
\tag{U.73b.3.2}
$$
$$
D^2S(\phi_*)\bigl[u\phi_*-\tau\,x\cdot\nabla\phi_*,\;u'\phi_*-\tau'\,x\cdot\nabla\phi_*\bigr]
=\sum_{j=1}^mf_j\,\bigl(w_j\cdot(u,\tau)\bigr)\bigl(w_j\cdot(u',\tau')\bigr).
\tag{U.73b.3.3}
$$
The weight-$\alpha$ dilation tangent $s_\alpha:=-\alpha\phi_*-x\cdot\nabla\phi_*$ corresponds to $(u,\tau)=(-\alpha,1)$ and has self-pairing $\sum_jf_jc_j(\alpha)^2$. When only the spatial law $F_j[\Phi_{0,\tau}\phi]=e^{(D-q_j)\tau}F_j[\phi]$ is available, the $\tau$-components of (U.73b.3.2)--(U.73b.3.3) remain valid; for the kinetic and subtracted-potential terms of Definition U.4 they are the virial identity of Theorem U.8a and the value $-4S_{\mathrm{kin}}(1)$ of Theorem U.8c.

3. The determinant of the $2\times2$ matrix $\sum_jf_jw_jw_j^{\mathsf T}$ in (U.73b.3.3) is
$$
\sum_{i<j}f_if_j\,(w_i\times w_j)^2,
\qquad w\times w':=w^{1}w'^{2}-w^{2}w'^{1}.
\tag{U.73b.3.4}
$$
If $u\phi_*-\tau\,x\cdot\nabla\phi_*$ is a nonzero Hessian-form kernel vector, then $(u,\tau)$ lies in the kernel of that matrix and (U.73b.3.4) vanishes.

4. If $m=2$ and $(f_1,f_2)\ne(0,0)$, then $w_1$ and $w_2$ are proportional, $S$ has the weighted-dilation symmetry of item 1, the matrix $\sum_jf_jw_jw_j^{\mathsf T}$ has rank one, and its kernel is spanned by $(-\alpha,1)$, the coordinate of $s_\alpha$. A two-term action without weighted-dilation symmetry therefore has no critical point with $(f_1,f_2)\ne(0,0)$ at which the hypotheses of item 2 hold.

*Proof.* Item 1. Since $T^{(\alpha)}_\rho=\Phi_{-\alpha\ln\rho,\ln\rho}$, (U.73b.3.1) gives $S[T^{(\alpha)}_\rho\phi]=\sum_j\rho^{c_j(\alpha)}F_j[\phi]$, so vanishing of every $c_j(\alpha)$ gives invariance. Conversely, assume invariance, fix $j$ and choose $\phi_j\in\mathcal D$ with $F_j[\phi_j]\ne0$. Invariance applied to $\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi_j$ gives
$$
\sum_ie^{w_i\cdot(u,\tau)}F_i[\phi_j]\bigl(\rho^{c_i(\alpha)}-1\bigr)=0
\qquad((u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^2).
$$
Exponentials with distinct frequency vectors are linearly independent: on a line $(u,\tau)=t\theta$ along which the numbers $w_i\cdot\theta$ are distinct, the largest exponent dominates as $t\to\infty$, and induction removes the terms one at a time. Hence $F_j[\phi_j](\rho^{c_j(\alpha)}-1)=0$ for every $\rho>0$, so $c_j(\alpha)=0$. The identity $c_j(\alpha)=p_j\bigl((D-q_j)/p_j-\alpha\bigr)$ gives the proportionality statement, uniqueness and the listed cases; for bidegrees $(2,2)$ and $(2,4)$ the equations $D-2\alpha-2=0$ and $D-2\alpha-4=0$ are incompatible.

Item 2. Put $G(u,\tau):=S[\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi_*]=\sum_je^{w_j\cdot(u,\tau)}f_j$. The chain rule and $DS(\phi_*)=0$ give $\nabla G(0)=0$, which is (U.73b.3.2). The second-order chain rule gives
$$
D^2G(0)[\xi,\xi']=D^2S(\phi_*)[D\Phi\,\xi,D\Phi\,\xi']+DS(\phi_*)[D^2\Phi(\xi,\xi')],
\qquad
D\Phi(u,\tau)=u\phi_*-\tau\,x\cdot\nabla\phi_*,
$$
whose last term vanishes; differentiating the exponential sum twice gives (U.73b.3.3), and $w_j\cdot(-\alpha,1)=c_j(\alpha)$. The $\tau$-components use only $\Phi_{0,\tau}$. For Definition U.4 the kinetic and subtracted-potential integrals have $D-q=2$ and $D-q=4$, so the $\tau$-component of (U.73b.3.2) reads $2S_{\mathrm{kin}}+4S_{\mathrm{pot}}=0$, and that of (U.73b.3.3) gives $4S_{\mathrm{kin}}+16S_{\mathrm{pot}}=-4S_{\mathrm{kin}}$.

Item 3. Equation (U.73b.3.4) is the Cauchy--Binet formula for $\det\sum_jf_jw_jw_j^{\mathsf T}$. A kernel vector $v=u\phi_*-\tau\,x\cdot\nabla\phi_*$ satisfies $D^2S(\phi_*)[v,v']=0$ for every $v'$ in the span of $\phi_*$ and $x\cdot\nabla\phi_*$, so by (U.73b.3.3) the vector $(u,\tau)$, nonzero because $v\ne0$, lies in the kernel of the matrix.

Item 4. If $f_1=0$, then (U.73b.3.2) gives $f_2w_2=0$, hence $f_2=0$ because $p_2>0$. Therefore $f_1f_2\ne0$ and $w_2=\mu w_1$ with $\mu=-f_1/f_2$, and $\mu>0$ because $p_1,p_2>0$. Item 1 gives the symmetry, with $c_1(\alpha)=c_2(\alpha)=0$. The matrix equals $(f_1+f_2\mu^2)w_1w_1^{\mathsf T}=f_1(1-\mu)w_1w_1^{\mathsf T}$, and $\mu\ne1$ because the bidegrees are distinct, so its rank is one and its kernel is the orthogonal complement of $w_1$, which contains $(-\alpha,1)$. ∎

<a id="theorem-u73b3a-full-hessian-amplitude-dilation-classification-for-three-nonzero-terms"></a>**Theorem U.73b.3a (Full-Hessian Amplitude--Dilation Classification for Three Nonzero Terms).** Use the action $S=\sum_jF_j$, weights $w_j=(p_j,D-q_j)$, critical point $\phi_*$ and admissible orbit of Theorem U.73b.3. Assume each $F_j$ is $C^2$ on the open field domain in $X$, every $\Phi_{u,\tau}$ is a bounded linear isomorphism of $X$ preserving that domain, and the action of this group on $X$ is strongly continuous. Define
$$
g_j=DF_j(\phi_*),\qquad v_\xi=u\phi_*-\tau x\cdot\nabla\phi_*,\qquad
\xi=(u,\tau),\qquad B=\sum_jf_jw_jw_j^{\mathsf T}.
$$
The statements below first concern the full Hessian form on $X$. For operator conclusions, require a continuous dense inclusion $X\subset\mathcal H$, a declared self-adjoint Hessian $L$, the relevant tangents in $\operatorname{Dom}L$, and $D^2S(\phi_*)[v,\eta]=\langle Lv,\eta\rangle_{\mathcal H}$ for each such tangent and every $\eta\in X$.

1. The exact full-Hessian identity is
$$
D^2S(\phi_*)[v_\xi,\eta]=\sum_j(w_j\cdot\xi)g_j[\eta]\qquad(\eta\in X).
$$
If $\dim\operatorname{span}\{g_j\}=m-1$, a tangent lies in the full form kernel exactly when all $w_j\cdot\xi$ equal one common value $\kappa$. This common degree gives
$$
S[\Phi_{tu,t\tau}\phi]=e^{\kappa t}S[\phi]
$$
throughout the domain and sends every full critical point to a full critical point. Action invariance is the case $\kappa=0$.

2. For an action with exactly three terms, suppose $f_1f_2f_3\ne0$ and the weights span $\mathbb R^2$. Relabel so $\Delta=w_1\times w_2\ne0$, and write $w_3=aw_1+bw_2$. Then $a,b\ne0$, $f_1=-af_3$, $f_2=-bf_3$, and
$$
\det B=f_3^2ab(1-a-b)\Delta^2
=\frac{f_1f_2}{f_3}S[\phi_*]\Delta^2.
$$
The tangent map is injective and $\dim\operatorname{span}\{g_1,g_2,g_3\}=2$. If $S[\phi_*]\ne0$, the full Hessian has no nonzero amplitude--dilation kernel tangent. If $S[\phi_*]=0$, then $a+b=1$ and
$$
B=f_3a(a-1)(w_1-w_2)(w_1-w_2)^{\mathsf T}.
$$
Its rank is one, and its kernel is exactly the coordinate space of the full-Hessian kernel tangents. For every nonzero $\xi$ with $(w_1-w_2)\cdot\xi=0$, the three degrees coincide at a nonzero value $\kappa$, yielding an exact relative-scaling critical family. Thus singularity of this reduced block is sufficient for full-Hessian survival on the stated three-term branch.

3. If all weights are proportional, put $\alpha_0=(D-q_j)/p_j$. For any number of terms, the full kernel within the amplitude--dilation tangent space is the image of
$$
\left\{(u,\tau):(u+\alpha_0\tau)\sum_jp_jg_j=0\right\}.
$$
It contains the invariant direction $(-\alpha_0,1)$ and is the whole tangent space exactly when $\sum_jp_jg_j=0$.

For a bounded, $C^1$, nonconstant radial profile, the tangent map is injective. A nonzero surviving tangent is independent of the translations: it is even under $x\mapsto-x$, whereas translation tangents are odd. In $D=4$, additionally suppose translations act as bounded linear isomorphisms of $X$ preserving the domain and action, the translated orbit of $\phi_*$ is $C^1$ into $X$, and its four tangents satisfy the same operator-domain conditions. Then a surviving radial tangent is a fifth independent operator zero mode. Other shape directions are covered by their own spectral analysis; Proposition U.73b.4a supplies an example with an invertible amplitude--dilation block and additional shape zero modes.

*Proof.* Fix $\xi$ and write $T_t=\Phi_{tu,t\tau}$. Differentiate the scaling identity for each $F_j$ with respect to the field, using bounded linearity of $T_t$:
$$
DS[T_t\phi_*][T_t\eta]=\sum_je^{t w_j\cdot\xi}g_j[\eta].
$$
The full equation $DS(\phi_*)=0$ makes its constant term zero. Since $T_t\phi_*=\phi_*+tv_\xi+o(t)$ in $X$, twice differentiability gives $DS[T_t\phi_*]=tD^2S(\phi_*)[v_\xi,\cdot]+o(t)$ in $X^*$. Strong continuity gives $T_t\eta\to\eta$. Dividing by $t$ and taking the limit proves item 1 without requiring differentiation of test vectors under dilations. The map $(c_j)\mapsto\sum_jc_jg_j$ has kernel spanned by $(1,\ldots,1)$ under the rank hypothesis, because $\sum_jg_j=0$. This proves the stated equivalence. Common degree gives the action law term by term; its field derivative is $DS[T_t\phi]\circ T_t=e^{\kappa t}DS[\phi]$, and invertibility of $T_t$ transports the full critical equation.

For item 2, the virial relation gives $(f_1+af_3)w_1+(f_2+bf_3)w_2=0$. Independence yields the asserted coefficients, and their nonzero values imply $a,b\ne0$. With $W=(w_1\ w_2)$,
$$
B=f_3W\begin{pmatrix}a(a-1)&ab\\ab&b(b-1)\end{pmatrix}W^{\mathsf T}.
$$
The central determinant is $ab(1-a-b)$, and $S[\phi_*]=f_3(1-a-b)$, proving both determinant formulas. Also $g_j[v_\xi]=f_j(w_j\cdot\xi)$ by differentiation along the orbit. Thus $v_\xi=0$ forces $\xi=0$, and the restricted covectors have rank two. Their full span has rank two because $\sum_jg_j=0$. Every full kernel tangent has $B\xi=0$, which excludes it when the determinant is nonzero. If $S[\phi_*]=0$, substitute $b=1-a$ to obtain the displayed rank-one matrix; its coefficient is nonzero. A coordinate vector in its kernel has equal inner products with $w_1,w_2,w_3$. Their common value cannot vanish unless $\xi=0$, since $w_1,w_2$ are independent. Item 1 proves full-Hessian survival and the critical family, establishing both directions.

For item 3, write $w_j=p_j(1,\alpha_0)$ in item 1. This gives exactly the displayed covector and its kernel. For radial injectivity, $u h-\tau rh'=0$ with $\tau\ne0$ gives $h(r)=Cr^{u/\tau}$, which is constant or zero if bounded at both zero and infinity; the case $\tau=0$ gives $u=0$. The four translations in $D=4$ are independent: a relation $a\cdot\nabla\phi_*=0$, evaluated on a radius where $h'\ne0$ and all its angular directions, gives $a=0$. Parity proves independence of a surviving radial tangent. The invertible translation maps transport the full critical equation, and differentiation of the admitted $C^1$ orbit makes its four tangents Hessian-form null. The stated representation of the second variation pairs its operator image to zero with the dense test space $X$, so a tangent in $\operatorname{Dom}L$ is an actual operator zero mode. ∎

**Nonvacuity of the relative-scaling branch.** In $D=4$, on $H^3(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R)\setminus\{0\}$, define
$$
K[\phi]=\frac12\int|\nabla\phi|^2,\qquad P[\phi]=\int\phi^6,\qquad
S[\phi]=K-2P+P^2/K=(K-P)^2/K.
$$
Fourier Cauchy--Schwarz and $\int(1+|k|^2)^{-3}d^4k<\infty$ give $H^3\subset L^\infty\cap L^2$, so $P$ is a continuous polynomial. Vanishing of $K$ would make an $L^2$ field constant, hence zero. Thus these functionals are $C^2$ on the declared open domain. The identities
$$
\|\partial^\beta\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi\|_2^2=e^{2u+(4-2|\beta|)\tau}\|\partial^\beta\phi\|_2^2\qquad(|\beta|\le3)
$$
give bounded invertibility and local uniform bounds. Density of compactly supported smooth functions proves strong continuity; the Gaussian orbit is $C^2$ by its polynomial-times-Gaussian derivatives. The weights are $(2,2),(6,4),(10,6)$, with common degree $1$ for $\xi=(-1/2,1)$.

At $\phi_*=\sqrt3e^{-|x|^2/2}$, direct Gaussian integration gives $K=P=3\pi^2$. It is a full critical point with term values $(3\pi^2,-6\pi^2,3\pi^2)$ and action zero. Set $h=-\Delta\phi_*-6\phi_*^5\in L^2$. Differentiating $(K-P)^2/K$ at $K=P$ gives
$$
D^2S(\phi_*)[\eta,\zeta]=\frac{2}{K[\phi_*]}\langle h,\eta\rangle\langle h,\zeta\rangle.
$$
Its $L^2$ realization is the bounded self-adjoint operator $2|h\rangle\langle h|/K[\phi_*]$ on all of $L^2$. The radial tangent $(|x|^2-1/2)\phi_*$ and the four translations are normalizable independent kernel directions. The critical value is zero and the full kernel is infinite-dimensional; this witness realizes the relative-scaling branch of the theorem.

**Four-term failure of the reduced-block converse.** On the same field domain, let $I[\phi]=\int\phi^4$ and define
$$
a=\frac{\log(P/(3\pi^2))-2\log(K/(3\pi^2))}{2},\qquad
b=\frac{3\log(K/(3\pi^2))-\log(P/(3\pi^2))}{2},\qquad
z=4\pi^2I/K^2-1,
$$
$$
\widetilde S=(-1+z)e^{a-2b}+(3-z)e^{a-b}+e^{a+b}-e^{3a}.
$$
All these functionals are $C^2$, since $K,P>0$ for a nonzero field. The transformation $\Phi_{u,\tau}$ sends $(a,b,z)$ to $(a+u,b+\tau,z)$, so the four weights are $(1,-2),(1,-1),(1,1),(3,0)$. At the same Gaussian, $I=9\pi^2/4$ and $(a,b,z)=(0,0,0)$. The gradient of $\widetilde S$ in these coordinates vanishes, its term values are $(-1,3,1,-1)$, its action is $2$, and its coordinate Hessian is
$$
H_{a,b,z}=\begin{pmatrix}-6&0&0\\0&0&-1\\0&-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Thus the field is a full critical point and the amplitude--dilation block is $\operatorname{diag}(-6,0)$, whereas
$$
D^2\widetilde S(\phi_*)[v_{(u,\tau)},\eta]=-6u\,Da(\phi_*)[\eta]-\tau\,Dz(\phi_*)[\eta].
$$
The covectors $Da,Db$ are an invertible recombination of $DK,DP$, and $Dz$ contains $DI$ with nonzero coefficient. At the Gaussian their $L^2$ gradients span $(4-|x|^2)\phi_*$, $\phi_*^5$ and $\phi_*^3$. These are independent: divide a putative relation by $\phi_*$, let $|x|\to\infty$ to eliminate its polynomial coefficient, and then use the different exponential decay rates to eliminate the remaining two coefficients. Hence $Da,Dz$ are independent and no nonzero amplitude--dilation tangent belongs to the full kernel. Pulling the displayed real symmetric matrix back by those three $L^2$ gradients gives a bounded finite-rank self-adjoint Hessian. This is a four-term scalar-field counterexample to the reduced-block converse; its separate shape kernel does not change the failed amplitude--dilation lift.

<a id="theorem-u73b3b-sharp-bidegree-data-survival-classification"></a>**Theorem U.73b.3b (Sharp Bidegree-Data Survival Classification).** Let $D,m\ge1$ be integers. Let $w_j=(p_j,D-q_j)\in\mathbb R^2$, $p_j>0$, be pairwise distinct, and let $W$ be the $m\times2$ matrix whose $j$th row is $w_j^{\mathsf T}$. Write $\mathbf1=(1,\ldots,1)^{\mathsf T}$. Prescribe $f\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfying
$$
W^{\mathsf T}f=0,
$$
and define
$$
B=W^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{diag}(f)W,
\qquad
E=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^2:W\xi\in\mathbb R\mathbf1\}
=\bigcap_{j=2}^m\ker (w_j-w_1)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad Z=\ker B.
$$
For $m=1$, the intersection defining $E$ is $\mathbb R^2$.

**Repeated-degree normalization.** As in Theorem U.73b.3, first combine all functionals of each equal bidegree and discard an aggregate only when it vanishes identically on the field domain. Its critical value is the sum of the original values in that class. A zero critical value alone does not justify discarding a term. Apply the theorem to the retained distinct bidegrees and their aggregate values; identically canceled aggregates impose no constraint on $E$. If every aggregate cancels, then $S\equiv0$ and every admissible amplitude--dilation tangent is in the full form kernel (and in the operator kernel under the declared domain and representation hypotheses); this empty-list case is separate from $m\ge1$.

**Necessity.** Consider any action $S=\sum_{j=1}^mF_j$ satisfying the bihomogeneity and differentiability hypotheses of Theorem U.73b.3a, at a critical point $\phi_*$ with $F_j(\phi_*)=f_j$. Assume its amplitude–dilation tangent map
$$
\xi=(u,\tau)\longmapsto v_\xi=u\phi_*-\tau x\cdot\nabla\phi_*
$$
is injective. Let
$$
K_S=\{\xi:D^2S(\phi_*)[v_\xi,\eta]=0\text{ for every }\eta\in X\}.
$$
Then
$$
E\subseteq K_S\subseteq Z.
\tag{U.73b.3b.1}
$$
The same assertion holds for the operator kernel when the tangents and second variation satisfy the operator-domain and representation hypotheses of Theorem U.73b.3a.

**Sufficiency and coverage.** For every subspace $K$ satisfying $E\subseteq K\subseteq Z$, there are $C^\infty$ functionals $F_1,\ldots,F_m$ on
$$
\mathcal D=H^s(\mathbb R^D;\mathbb R)\setminus\{0\},\qquad s\in\mathbb N,\ s>D/2
$$
such that:

1. Each $F_j$ is nonzero as a functional, Euclidean invariant, and has exactly the prescribed bidegree $(p_j,q_j)$.
2. At $g(x)=e^{-|x|^2/2}$, the full action is critical and $F_j(g)=f_j$.
3. Its second variation at $g$ extends to a bounded finite-rank self-adjoint operator on real $L^2(\mathbb R^D)$, with domain all of $L^2$.
4. Its full form and operator kernels meet the amplitude–dilation tangent plane in exactly $\{v_\xi:\xi\in K\}$.
5. The $D$ translations are independent operator zero modes. Every nonzero tangent in item 4 is independent of those translations; for $D=4$ it supplies a fifth direction. The choice $s=3$ is available in $D=4$.

Consequently, (U.73b.3b.1) lists every possible amplitude–dilation survival space for fixed $(W,f)$ in this original bihomogeneous action class. A direction outside $Z$ is excluded for every such action; a direction in $E$ survives for every such action; a direction in $Z\setminus E$ survives for one such action and fails to survive for another with identical $(W,f)$. In particular, those data determine $K_S$ for all compatible actions exactly when $E=Z$.

*Proof.*

**1. Universal inclusions.**

Put $g_j=DF_j(\phi_*)\in X^*$. Criticality gives $\sum_jg_j=0$. For $T_t=\Phi_{tu,t\tau}$, differentiate bihomogeneity with respect to the field to obtain
$$
DS(T_t\phi_*)[T_t\eta]
=\sum_je^{t w_j\cdot\xi}g_j[\eta].
$$
