Here each $T_t$ is a bounded linear isomorphism, the orbit of $\phi_*$ is differentiable in $X$, and $T_t\eta\to\eta$ by strong continuity. Since $DS(\phi_*)=0$, the left side divided by $t$ converges to $D^2S(\phi_*)[v_\xi,\eta]$. The constant term on the right vanishes. Therefore
$$
D^2S(\phi_*)[v_\xi,\eta]
=\sum_j(w_j\cdot\xi)g_j[\eta].
\tag{U.73b.3b.2}
$$
If $\xi\in E$, the coefficients in (U.73b.3b.2) have one common value, so the sum is zero. Thus $E\subseteq K_S$. Differentiating each term along another orbit tangent gives
$$
g_j[v_\zeta]=f_j(w_j\cdot\zeta).
$$
Substitute this into (U.73b.3b.2). If $\xi\in K_S$, then $\xi^{\mathsf T}B\zeta=0$ for every $\zeta$, hence $\xi\in Z$. The identity $B\xi=\kappa W^{\mathsf T}f=0$ whenever $W\xi=\kappa\mathbf1$ also verifies $E\subseteq Z$ directly.

For the operator assertion, membership of the tangent in the declared domain and the second-variation identity give $\langle Lv_\xi,\eta\rangle=0$ for a dense set of $\eta$ exactly when the full form annihilates that tangent. This is equivalent to $Lv_\xi=0$.

**2. A finite separating matrix.**

Fix $E\subseteq K\subseteq Z$ and let $r=\dim Z-\dim K$, so $0\le r\le2$. Let $\pi:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m/\mathbb R\mathbf1$ be the quotient map. On $Z$, the map $\pi W$ has kernel exactly $E$. Consequently it induces an injective map from $Z/E$ into that quotient. Choose a surjective linear map $\ell:Z/E\to\mathbb R^r$ with kernel $K/E$. Its coordinate functionals extend from the finite-dimensional subspace $\pi W(Z)$ to all of $\mathbb R^m/\mathbb R\mathbf1$: extend any basis of that subspace to a basis of the quotient and set the additional coefficients to zero. Lifting the extended functionals to $\mathbb R^m$ gives a real $r\times m$ matrix $A$ with
$$
A\mathbf1=0,
\qquad
\ker B\cap\ker(AW)=K.
\tag{U.73b.3b.3}
$$
For $r=0$, $A$ has no rows and the second kernel is all of $\mathbb R^2$.

**3. Smooth global amplitude, dilation and shape coordinates.**

On $\mathcal D$, define
$$
\mathcal K[\phi]=\int_{\mathbb R^D}|\nabla\phi|^2\,dx,
\qquad
\mathcal N[\phi]=\int_{\mathbb R^D}\phi^2\,dx,
\qquad
I_\ell[\phi]=\int_{\mathbb R^D}\phi^{2\ell}\,dx\quad(\ell\ge2).
$$
The continuous inclusion $H^s\subset L^\infty\cap L^2$ follows from Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz and $\int_{\mathbb R^D}(1+|k|^2)^{-s}dk<\infty$. Each $I_\ell$ is a continuous homogeneous polynomial on $H^s$: its associated $2\ell$-linear integral is bounded by placing two arguments in $L^2$ and the others in $L^\infty$. Hence all displayed functionals are $C^\infty$. Also $\mathcal N>0$ on $\mathcal D$, and $\mathcal K=0$ would make a field constant almost everywhere and therefore zero in $L^2$. Thus $\mathcal K>0$ there.

Gaussian integration gives
$$
\mathcal N[g]=\pi^{D/2},\qquad
\mathcal K[g]=\frac D2\pi^{D/2},\qquad
I_\ell[g]=\frac{\pi^{D/2}}{\ell^{D/2}}.
\tag{U.73b.3b.4}
$$
Put $k=\log(\mathcal K/\mathcal K[g])$, $n=\log(\mathcal N/\mathcal N[g])$ and
$$
a=\frac{Dk-(D-2)n}{4},\qquad b=\frac12(n-k),
$$
$$
z_\ell=
\frac{I_\ell}{I_\ell[g]}
\left(\frac{\mathcal K}{\mathcal K[g]}\right)^{D(1-\ell)/2}
\left(\frac{\mathcal N}{\mathcal N[g]}\right)^{((D-2)\ell-D)/2}-1.
\tag{U.73b.3b.5}
$$
All these are smooth on the full open domain $\mathcal D$ and vanish at $g$. Under $\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi=e^u\phi(e^{-\tau}\,\cdot)$,
$$
\mathcal K\mapsto e^{2u+(D-2)\tau}\mathcal K,
\quad
\mathcal N\mapsto e^{2u+D\tau}\mathcal N,
\quad
I_\ell\mapsto e^{2\ell u+D\tau}I_\ell.
$$
It follows directly that
$$
a\mapsto a+u,\qquad b\mapsto b+\tau,\qquad z_\ell\mapsto z_\ell.
\tag{U.73b.3b.6}
$$
Translations and orthogonal transformations preserve all these scalar functionals.

We shall use $z_2,\ldots,z_{r+2}$. The covectors
$$
Da(g),\ Db(g),\ Dz_2(g),\ldots,Dz_{r+2}(g)
\tag{U.73b.3b.7}
$$
are linearly independent and have radial Schwartz $L^2$ representing vectors. Indeed
$$
D\mathcal N(g)[h]=2\langle g,h\rangle,
\quad
D\mathcal K(g)[h]=2\langle(D-|x|^2)g,h\rangle,
\quad
DI_\ell(g)[h]=2\ell\langle g^{2\ell-1},h\rangle.
$$
The first two in (U.73b.3b.7) are an invertible recombination of $D\mathcal K(g),D\mathcal N(g)$. Each successive $Dz_\ell(g)$ contains $DI_\ell(g)/I_\ell[g]$ with nonzero coefficient and otherwise only the first two covectors. Independence therefore reduces to that of
$$
g,\quad |x|^2g,\quad g^3,\quad g^5,\ldots,g^{2r+3}.
$$
If a real linear combination vanishes, divide by the everywhere-positive $g$ and set $R=|x|^2$. It becomes a polynomial of degree at most one plus a combination of $e^{-R},e^{-2R},\ldots,e^{-(r+1)R}$. Letting $R\to\infty$ first annihilates both polynomial coefficients. Multiplying the remaining identity by $e^R$ and passing to infinity annihilates its first exponential coefficient; repeat to annihilate the rest. This proves independence.

In particular, the coordinate map in (U.73b.3b.7) has surjective derivative onto $\mathbb R^{r+3}$. To see that its image contains an open neighborhood of zero without any infinite-dimensional inverse theorem, choose $r+3$ directions on which the derivative matrix is invertible and restrict the map to the affine space through $g$ spanned by them. The ordinary inverse-function theorem applies on that finite-dimensional space.

**4. The realizing action and its complete tangent test.**

For the matrix in (U.73b.3b.3), set
$$
F_j[\phi]=
\exp\bigl(p_ja[\phi]+(D-q_j)b[\phi]\bigr)
\left(f_j+\sum_{\ell=1}^r A_{\ell j}z_{\ell+1}[\phi]
       +z_{r+2}[\phi]^2\right).
\tag{U.73b.3b.8}
$$
Formula (U.73b.3b.6) gives the required bidegree identity for every field in $\mathcal D$ and every $(u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^2$. Euclidean invariance and smoothness follow from those of the coordinates. Each coefficient polynomial in (U.73b.3b.8) is nonzero, including when $f_j=0$ and all $A_{\ell j}=0$, because its $z_{r+2}^2$ coefficient is one. The local open-image property just proved shows that none of these functionals vanishes identically. Distinct prescribed bidegrees therefore remain distinct nonzero terms. A nonzero functional cannot have two different bidegrees, because the two exponential scaling factors would have to agree for every $(u,\tau)$ at a field where it is nonzero.

Write $x=(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2$, $z=(z_2,\ldots,z_{r+1})\in\mathbb R^r$, and $z_0=z_{r+2}$. As a function of these coordinates, the action is
$$
\mathcal S(x,z,z_0)=\sum_j e^{w_j\cdot x}(f_j+A_{\cdot j}\cdot z+z_0^2).
$$
At $(0,0,0)$ its coordinate gradient is $(W^{\mathsf T}f,A\mathbf1,0)=0$, so $DS(g)=0$ on the entire field space. Its coordinate Hessian is the real symmetric matrix
$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}
B&W^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}&0\\
AW&0&0\\
0&0&2m
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{U.73b.3b.9}
$$
Because the coordinate gradient vanishes, the second-order chain rule has no coordinate-second-derivative term. If $J$ is the derivative at $g$ of the coordinate map, then
$$
D^2S(g)[h,\widetilde h]=(Jh)^{\mathsf T}M(J\widetilde h).
\tag{U.73b.3b.10}
$$
Every row of $J$ is represented by a Schwartz vector. Consequently $J$ extends to a bounded map from real $L^2$ to $\mathbb R^{r+3}$, and
$$
L=J^*MJ
\tag{U.73b.3b.11}
$$
is a bounded finite-rank self-adjoint operator on all of real $L^2$.

At the Gaussian, $v_\xi=(u+\tau|x|^2)g$. Formula (U.73b.3b.6) gives $Jv_\xi=(\xi,0,0)$. Hence (U.73b.3b.9)–(U.73b.3b.10) imply
$$
D^2S(g)[v_\xi,h]
=(B\xi)\cdot D(a,b)(g)[h]
 +(AW\xi)\cdot D(z_2,\ldots,z_{r+1})(g)[h].
$$
The covectors in (U.73b.3b.7) are independent, so this vanishes for every $h\in H^s$ exactly when $B\xi=0$ and $AW\xi=0$. By (U.73b.3b.3), that is exactly $\xi\in K$. Density of $H^s$ in $L^2$ and (U.73b.3b.11) give the identical operator-kernel condition.

Finally $t_i=\partial_i g=-x_ig$ are independent Schwartz functions. Every row of $J$ is radial, so $Jt_i=0$ and $Lt_i=0$. The map $\xi\mapsto (u+\tau|x|^2)g$ is injective. Its nonzero images are even, whereas the translations are odd; thus each surviving image is an independent additional direction (a fifth when $D=4$).

For completeness, the scaling maps preserve $H^s\setminus\{0\}$ and are bounded linear isomorphisms. For $|\beta|\le s$,
$$
\|\partial^\beta\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi\|_2^2
=e^{2u+(D-2|\beta|)\tau}\|\partial^\beta\phi\|_2^2.
$$
These identities give locally uniform bounds. Strong continuity follows first for compactly supported smooth fields by differentiation and domination, and then for every $H^s$ field by density and those bounds. The Gaussian amplitude–dilation and translation orbits are $C^\infty$ into $H^s$, since their parameter derivatives are polynomial-times-Gaussian functions locally dominated in every derivative through order $s$. Thus all original orbit-admissibility hypotheses hold.

This proves the realizing theorem. Taking $K=E$ and $K=Z$ proves the final trichotomy, including the two different answers for every $\xi\in Z\setminus E$. $\square$

**Scope of the classification and its realizations.** The theorem classifies exactly the intersection of the full Hessian kernel with the amplitude--dilation tangent plane for fixed normalized $(W,f)$; it does not classify the remaining shape kernel of an arbitrary action. In the realizing actions, $\ker J\subseteq\ker L$ is infinite-dimensional, already within the radial sector, because $J$ has finite-dimensional range. Consequently these finite-rank $L^2$ Hessians have infinite nullity and are not Fredholm. Even a realization with $K=\{0\}$ therefore has additional shape zero modes. The realizations therefore carry no finite-nullity, Fredholm or compact-orbit record of Definition U.16b.

<a id="proposition-u73b4-symmetry-generated-collective-orbits-of-radial-critical-points"></a>**Proposition U.73b.4 (Symmetry-Generated Collective Orbits of Radial Critical Points).** Let $\phi_*$ be a bounded continuous nonconstant function on $\mathbb R^D$ that is radial about the origin, let $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, and let each similarity $\sigma(x)=\rho Rx+b$, with $\rho>0$, $R\in O(D)$ and $b\in\mathbb R^D$, act by $(T_\sigma\phi)(x):=\rho^{-\alpha}\phi(\sigma^{-1}x)$. If $T_\sigma\phi_*=\phi_*$, then $\rho=1$. Consequently, for a continuous one-parameter group $\sigma_t$ of similarities, the orbit $t\mapsto T_{\sigma_t}\phi_*$ is periodic only when every $\sigma_t$ is a Euclidean motion, and then $T_{\sigma_t}\phi_*=\phi_*(\cdot-\sigma_t(0))$ lies in the translation family of $\phi_*$, with tangent in $\operatorname{span}\{\partial_\mu\phi_*\}$ when $\phi_*$ is $C^1$. A compact one-dimensional orbit of a one-parameter group is periodic. Hence, for an action invariant under Euclidean motions and, when present, under the weighted dilations of Theorem U.73b.3, no one-parameter group of these symmetries has a compact one-dimensional orbit through a radial critical point outside its translation family, and the compact fifth direction of Definition U.16b requires an additional symmetry or a critical manifold not generated by symmetry.

*Proof.* The rule $\sigma\mapsto T_\sigma$ is a group action, since the dilation factor of $\sigma\sigma'$ is $\rho\rho'$. Suppose $T_\sigma\phi_*=\phi_*$ with $\rho\ne1$. Replacing $\sigma$ by $\sigma^{-1}$ if necessary, assume $\rho>1$. Then $\sigma^{-1}$ is a contraction with a unique fixed point $x_0$, and iteration gives both $\phi_*(x)=\rho^{-n\alpha}\phi_*(\sigma^{-n}x)$, with $\sigma^{-n}x\to x_0$, and $\phi_*(x)=\rho^{n\alpha}\phi_*(\sigma^nx)$. For $\alpha>0$ the first identity and continuity give $\phi_*(x)=0$; for $\alpha=0$ they give $\phi_*(x)=\phi_*(x_0)$; for $\alpha<0$ the second identity and boundedness give $\phi_*(x)=0$. In each case $\phi_*$ would be constant. For a continuous one-parameter group, $\rho(t)=e^{\kappa t}$; if $\kappa\ne0$, then $T_{\sigma_T}\phi_*=\phi_*$ forces $T=0$. If $\kappa=0$, then $\sigma_t(x)=R_tx+b_t$ with $b_t=\sigma_t(0)$, and radiality gives $\phi_*(R_t^{-1}(x-b_t))=\phi_*(x-b_t)$, whose $t$-derivative is $-\dot b_t\cdot\nabla\phi_*(x-b_t)$. The stabilizer of $\phi_*$ in a one-parameter group is a closed subgroup of $\mathbb R$; if it were trivial, the orbit map $\gamma$ would be a continuous bijection of $\mathbb R$ onto a compact one-dimensional orbit, that is, onto a circle or a closed arc. No such bijection exists. Choose $t_0$ with $\gamma(t_0)$ an interior point, and use an arc coordinate on the complement of $\gamma(t_0)$ in the circle, or on the closed arc. A continuous injection of an open interval is strictly monotone in that coordinate with an open-interval image, so the images of $(-\infty,t_0)$ and $(t_0,\infty)$ are disjoint nonempty open intervals whose union is the complement of $\gamma(t_0)$. That complement is a connected open interval for a circle and contains the two endpoints for a closed arc; in neither case is it such a union. ∎

<a id="proposition-u73b4a-three-term-full-hessian-counterexample"></a>**Proposition U.73b.4a (Three-Term Full-Hessian Counterexample).** The broad bihomogeneous class of Theorem U.73b.3 admits positive-action critical points with additional full-Hessian zero modes even when the amplitude--dilation block is invertible. On $X=H^1(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R)$ define
$$
K[\phi]=\int|\nabla\phi|^2\,dx,\qquad N[\phi]=\int\phi^2\,dx,\qquad
S[\phi]=K[\phi]+N[\phi]-K[\phi]N[\phi].
$$
This is a smooth Euclidean-invariant action with distinct bidegrees $(2,2),(2,0),(4,-2)$ and no weighted-dilation symmetry. The radial Schwartz function
$$
\phi_*(x)=\frac1{2\pi}e^{-|x|^2/4}
$$
is critical with $K=N=S=1$. Writing $k=-\Delta\phi_*=(2-|x|^2/4)\phi_*$, its Hessian extends to the bounded self-adjoint operator
$$
H=-4\bigl(|k\rangle\langle\phi_*|+|\phi_*\rangle\langle k|\bigr)
$$
on real $L^2$, where $|a\rangle\langle b|$ denotes $h\mapsto a\langle b,h\rangle$. Its full kernel and spectrum are
$$
\ker H=\{\phi_*,k\}^{\perp},\qquad
\sigma(H)=\{-4-2\sqrt6,\ 0,\ -4+2\sqrt6\}.
$$
The nonzero eigenvalues are simple and zero has infinite multiplicity. The four translations $t_i=(x_i/2)\phi_*$ and the radial vector
$$
\zeta=(|x|^4-12|x|^2+24)\phi_*
$$
are independent kernel vectors. The amplitude--dilation matrix is
$$
\begin{pmatrix}-8&-12\\-12&-16\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det=-16.
$$
Near $\phi_*$ in $H^1$, the critical set is exactly the smooth codimension-two manifold $K=N=1$.

*Proof.* The action is a continuous polynomial of the two continuous quadratic forms on $H^1$, hence smooth. The scaling action of Theorem U.73b.3 gives factors $e^{2u+2\tau}$, $e^{2u+4\tau}$ and $e^{4u+6\tau}$ on its terms. Their scale weights $(2,2),(2,4),(4,6)$ are nonproportional, so the bidegree theorem excludes weighted-dilation symmetry. All terms are nonzero functionals on the scaling-invariant domain. Translation and orthogonal invariance follow from the integrals.

The density $\phi_*^2$ is that of four independent standard Gaussians. With $R=|x|^2$,
$$
\mathbb ER=4,\qquad\mathbb ER^2=24,\qquad\mathbb ER^3=192.
$$
Hence $N=1$ and $K=\mathbb ER/4=1$. Since $DS=(1-N)DK+(1-K)DN$, the point is critical and $S=1$. At this point
$$
D^2S[\eta,\xi]=-DK[\eta]DN[\xi]-DN[\eta]DK[\xi].
$$
Integration by parts gives $DK[\eta]=2\langle k,\eta\rangle$ and $DN[\eta]=2\langle\phi_*,\eta\rangle$ on $H^1$. Both representing vectors are Schwartz, proving the stated bounded $L^2$ extension and its uniqueness by density.

The Gram values are $\|\phi_*\|^2=\langle k,\phi_*\rangle=1$ and $\|k\|^2=3/2$. The pair $\phi_*,\sqrt2(k-\phi_*)$ is orthonormal, and on its span the Hessian is
$$
\begin{pmatrix}-8&-2\sqrt2\\-2\sqrt2&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2+8\lambda-8$, while the orthogonal complement is exactly the kernel. This proves the complete spectrum and negative index one. The translations are odd in their respective coordinates and orthogonal to the radial $k,\phi_*$. The identities $24-12\cdot4+24=0$ and $192-12\cdot24+24\cdot4=0$ put $\zeta$ orthogonal to $\phi_*$ and $R\phi_*$, hence to $k$. Its radial parity separates it from the translations, and its quadratic term in $R$ separates it from the amplitude--dilation span $\operatorname{span}\{\phi_*,R\phi_*\}$. Differentiating
$$
S[\Phi_{u,\tau}\phi_*]=e^{2u+2\tau}+e^{2u+4\tau}-e^{4u+6\tau}
$$
gives the displayed invertible scale block.

Finally, the derivative of $(K,N):H^1\to\mathbb R^2$ on directions $(\phi_*,k)$ has matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&3\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ of determinant $-2$. Continuity keeps $DK,DN$ independent in a neighborhood. There $DS=0$ is equivalent to $K=N=1$, and the Banach implicit-function theorem supplies the critical submanifold. Its tangent is the Hessian-form kernel in $H^1$, so every such tangent integrates to a smooth critical curve. ∎

This counterexample refutes universal fifth-mode exclusion on the class of Theorem U.73b.3 with at least three distinct terms, including the added requirements of positive critical action, radial rapid decay, Euclidean invariance, one negative direction and an invertible scale block. Its action is globally nonlocal and its full Hessian has infinite nullity. The exactly-five, compact-orbit and Fredholm requirements of Definition U.16b are addressed by the different action below.

<a id="theorem-u73b4b-logarithmic-action-with-a-compact-fifth-mode"></a>**Theorem U.73b.4b (Logarithmic Action with a Compact Fifth Mode).** For $D,m\ge1$, on real $m$-component fields define the finite-entropy domain and dimensionless action
$$
\mathscr E=\left\{\Phi\in H^1(\mathbb R^D;\mathbb R^m):\int |\Phi|^2\,|\log|\Phi|^2|\,dx<\infty\right\},
$$
$$
\mathcal S[\Phi]=\frac12\int\left[|\nabla\Phi|^2-|\Phi|^2\bigl(\log|\Phi|^2+D-1\bigr)\right]dx,
\qquad0\log0=0.
$$
At $\Phi_*=g e_1$, $g(x)=e^{-|x|^2/2}$, the action is $\pi^{D/2}/2$ and the genuine compact-test second variation closes on
$$
Q=\{h\in H^1(\mathbb R^D;\mathbb R^m):|x|h\in L^2\}
$$
to the self-adjoint operator
$$
\mathcal H=\operatorname{diag}(H_+,H_-,\ldots,H_-),\quad
H_+=-\Delta+|x|^2-D-2,\quad H_-=-\Delta+|x|^2-D.
$$
Its full kernel is
$$
\ker\mathcal H=\operatorname{span}\{x_i g e_1:1\le i\le D\}
\oplus\operatorname{span}\{g e_a:2\le a\le m\}.
$$
There is one negative eigenvalue $-2$, carried by $g e_1$, and the positive normal spectrum starts at $2$. The critical family
$$
\Phi_{a,v}(x)=e^{-|x-a|^2/2}v,\qquad a\in\mathbb R^D,\ v\in S^{m-1},
$$
has exactly this tangent space. In particular $D=4,m=2$ gives exactly five operator zero modes and a compact internal circle.

*Proof.* Compactly supported variations see a Gaussian bounded away from zero on their support, so differentiating the smooth integrand gives the Euler equation
$$
-\Delta\Phi-\bigl(D+\log|\Phi|^2\bigr)\Phi=0.
$$
The identities $-\Delta g=(D-|x|^2)g$ and $\log g^2=-|x|^2$ prove criticality. Gaussian integration gives $\|g\|_2^2=\pi^{D/2}$, $\int|\nabla g|^2=(D/2)\pi^{D/2}$ and the action value. Differentiating the nonlinear term gives
$$
-\bigl(D+\log|\Phi|^2\bigr)I_m-2\frac{\Phi\Phi^{\mathsf T}}{|\Phi|^2},
$$
which at $g e_1$ yields the stated Hessian. The oscillator form is closed on $Q$, compactly supported smooth functions are its form core, and the remaining matrix term is bounded. Thus its closure is the stated semibounded operator.

In one dimension, $a=\partial_x+x$ and $a^*=-\partial_x+x$ satisfy $-\partial_x^2+x^2=a^*a+1$, $[a,a^*]=2$, and $ag=0$. Their iterates give the Hermite eigenbasis; completeness follows from density of polynomials in Gaussian $L^2$, obtained by applying Fourier-transform injectivity to a function orthogonal to all polynomials using its Gaussian exponential moments. Tensor products give eigenvalue $2n+D$ at total Hermite degree $n$, with multiplicity $\binom{n+D-1}{D-1}$ for $D\ge2$ and one for $D=1$. The longitudinal eigenvalues are $2n-2$, and each transverse component has eigenvalues $2n$. The domain is the Hermite-coefficient domain with square-summable eigenvalue-weighted coefficients. These formulas give the full kernel, the one negative eigenvalue and the gap. Translation and global $O(m)$ invariance give the family; its modulus determines the center and its vector value then determines $v$, proving injectivity. Its Gaussian parametrization is smooth in the form and graph norms and has precisely the displayed tangents. ∎

<a id="theorem-u73b4c-gaussian-critical-family-completeness-in-a-smooth-chart"></a>**Theorem U.73b.4c (Gaussian Critical-Family Completeness in a Smooth Chart).** For $m=2$, identify the field with $\mathbb C$. Let $Y$ be the real Banach space of $C^4$ functions with norm
$$
\|u\|_Y=|u(0)|+|\nabla u(0)|+\sum_{j=2}^4\|D^j u\|_\infty,
$$
and let $Z=C_b^4(\mathbb R^D;\mathbb R)$, including boundedness of the function. Fix $0<\varepsilon<1$ and use the chart
$$
\Phi=e^{v+i\theta},\qquad v=-|x|^2/2+u,\quad
u\in Y,\quad\|D^2u\|_{\infty,\mathrm{op}}<\varepsilon,\quad\theta\in Z,
$$
where phases are identified by constant multiples of $2\pi$. The action is smooth in this chart and its critical set is exactly
$$
\Phi(x)=e^{-|x-a|^2/2}e^{i\theta_0},\qquad
(a,\theta_0)\in\mathbb R^D\times(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z).
$$

*Proof.* The curvature bound gives
$$
v(x)\le v(0)+\nabla v(0)\cdot x-\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2}|x|^2.
$$
Chart directions grow at most quadratically and their derivatives at most polynomially. On a small Banach neighborhood the curvature gap is uniformly positive. Polynomial Gaussian majorants for all derivatives of the action, together with Taylor's theorem, prove Fréchet smoothness. Every compactly supported smooth field variation is admitted by dividing by the nonzero field to obtain relative chart directions. Hence chart criticality gives the Euler equation.

Write $\rho=e^v$. Its real and imaginary parts are
$$
\Delta v+|\nabla v|^2-|\nabla\theta|^2+D+2v=0,
\qquad\operatorname{div}(\rho^2\nabla\theta)=0.
$$
Multiply the second equation by $\theta$ with compact cutoffs and let the cutoff radius grow. Boundedness of $\theta,\nabla\theta$ and Gaussian decay make the boundary terms vanish, giving $\int\rho^2|\nabla\theta|^2=0$. Thus $\theta$ is constant and $\Delta v+|\nabla v|^2+D+2v=0$. Put $A=D^2v$, $W=A+I$ and $L=-\Delta-2\nabla v\cdot\nabla$. Differentiating twice gives
$$
LA=2(A^2+A),\qquad LW=2(W^2-W).
$$
The divergence form $L=-\rho^{-2}\operatorname{div}(\rho^2\nabla)$ is symmetric in $L^2(\rho^2dx)$. Pairing with $W$ and removing cutoffs by the same bounds yields
$$
\int\rho^2|\nabla W|^2
=2\int\rho^2\bigl(\operatorname{tr}(W^3)-\|W\|_F^2\bigr)
\le-2(1-\varepsilon)\int\rho^2\|W\|_F^2.
$$
Every eigenvalue of $W=D^2u$ has absolute value below $\varepsilon$, proving the inequality. Therefore $W=0$ and $v=-|x-a|^2/2+c$; substitution fixes $c=0$. Conversely these fields solve the equation and Gaussian integration by parts proves stationarity against every chart direction. The inverse parametrization reads the affine part of $v+|x|^2/2$ and the constant phase, giving the stated smooth critical manifold. ∎

For $D=4,m=2$, set $t_i=x_i g e_1$, $\eta_5=g e_2$, $n_-=g e_1$. Their squared norms are $\pi^2/2,\pi^2,\pi^2$ respectively, and all six vectors are mutually orthogonal. Thus
$$
\Pi_0h=\frac2{\pi^2}\sum_{i=1}^4t_i\langle t_i,h\rangle
+\frac1{\pi^2}\eta_5\langle\eta_5,h\rangle,
\qquad\Pi_-h=\frac1{\pi^2}n_-\langle n_-,h\rangle.
$$
The positive normal inverse has norm $1/2$. The oscillator has compact resolvent; as a map from its graph domain to $L^2$, $\mathcal H$ has closed range, index zero, and kernel and cokernel dimension five. The induced collective metric and volume are
$$
ds^2=\frac{\pi^2}{2}\sum_{i=1}^4 da_i^2+\pi^2d\theta^2,
\qquad d\operatorname{vol}_{\mathrm{coll}}=\frac{\pi^5}{4}\,d^4a\,d\theta,
\quad0\le\theta<2\pi.
$$
The compact circle has circumference $2\pi^2$; the translation volume is separate. Equal fields have equal centers and phases modulo $2\pi$, so this measure has no additional overlap.

The logarithmic two-component action supplies the critical-manifold, full-kernel, projector, Fredholm and geometric-measure entries of Definition U.16b on the declared chart and oscillator domain. Its internal $O(2)$ action is global. Acceptance of the compact fifth-mode certificate additionally requires this tangent to survive the PU gauge and response quotient. Carrier marking, exponent calibration, determinant/remainder and physical realization retain their own records. The logarithmic vacuum singularity and confining oscillator asymptotics place this model in an action class distinct from the smooth positive-mass false-vacuum branch of Theorem U.13b.

<a id="theorem-u73b4d-subcritical-power-ground-state-orbits-and-their-complete-hessian"></a>**Theorem U.73b.4d (Subcritical-Power Ground-State Orbits and Their Complete Hessian).** Fix an integer $m\ge1$, $\omega>0$ and $1<p<3$. Use ordinary Euclidean volume, the real Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^m)$ and the action
$$
S_{\omega,p}[\Phi]=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\frac12|\nabla\Phi|^2+\frac\omega2|\Phi|^2-\frac1{p+1}|\Phi|^{p+1}\right)dx,
\qquad X=H^1(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^m).
\tag{U.73b.4d.1}
$$
Among measurable fields with weak first derivatives, separate finiteness of the three integrals is equivalent to membership in $X$, and $S_{\omega,p}$ is $C^2$ on this whole real Banach space. Let $u=u_{\omega,p}>0$ be the centered radial scalar ground state of
$$
-\Delta u+\omega u=u^p.
\tag{U.73b.4d.2}
$$
It exists, is strictly decreasing in $|x|>0$, and is the unique positive radial decaying solution with its center fixed. The uniqueness input is Kwong's positive-radial-solution theorem (Kwong, 1989); the existence and spectral assertions used here are proved below. Put
$$
M=\int u^2,\qquad G=\int|\nabla u|^2,\qquad P=\int u^{p+1},\qquad T=G/4.
$$
Then the following conclusions hold for every permitted $(m,\omega,p)$.

1. The ground-state symmetry orbit is
$$
\mathcal M=\{\Phi_{a,v}(x)=u(x-a)v:a\in\mathbb R^4,\ v\in S^{m-1}\}.
\tag{U.73b.4d.3}
$$
Every member is a vector Nehari minimizer. In a sufficiently small $H^1$ neighborhood of each member, these are all the critical points. Its scalar quantities obey
$$
G=\frac{2(p-1)}{p+1}P,\qquad
\omega M=\frac{3-p}{p+1}P,\qquad
S_{\omega,p}[\Phi_{a,v}]=T=\frac{p-1}{2(p+1)}P>0.
\tag{U.73b.4d.4}
$$

2. At $u e_1$ the form domain is $H^1$ and the self-adjoint Hessian has operator domain $H^2(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^m)$ and decomposition
$$
\mathcal H=\operatorname{diag}(L_+,L_-,\ldots,L_-),\quad
L_+=-\Delta+\omega-pu^{p-1},\quad
L_-=-\Delta+\omega-u^{p-1}.
\tag{U.73b.4d.5}
$$
Its full kernel and negative index are
$$
\ker\mathcal H=\operatorname{span}\{-\partial_i u\,e_1:1\le i\le4\}
\oplus\operatorname{span}\{u e_\alpha:2\le\alpha\le m\},
\qquad \operatorname{ind}_-(\mathcal H)=1.
\tag{U.73b.4d.6}
$$
Thus the nullity is $m+3$, and it equals five exactly when $m=2$. The unique negative eigenvalue $\lambda_-<0$ is simple, with a positive radial scalar eigenfunction $\psi_-$ normalized by $\|\psi_-\|_2=1$ in the first component. The essential spectrum is $[\omega,\infty)$. There is a number $\delta_{\omega,p}>0$ such that
$$
\langle h,\mathcal Hh\rangle\ge\delta_{\omega,p}\|h\|_2^2
\quad\text{for }h\in H^1,\quad
h\perp\ker\mathcal H,\quad h\perp\psi_-e_1.
\tag{U.73b.4d.7}
$$
Here the left side means the closed quadratic form. The number $\delta_{\omega,p}$ may be taken as the lower edge of the positive spectrum of $L_+\oplus L_-$. It is not an asserted uniform bound as $p$ approaches an excluded endpoint. On the graph domain, $\mathcal H:H^2\to L^2$ is Fredholm of index zero, with kernel and cokernel dimension $m+3$; its positive normal inverse has $L^2\to L^2$ operator norm at most $\delta_{\omega,p}^{-1}$.

3. Set $t_i=-\partial_i u\,e_1$ and $z_\alpha=u e_\alpha$. These vectors are mutually orthogonal, with $\|t_i\|_2^2=T$ and $\|z_\alpha\|_2^2=M$. The exact orthogonal projectors at $u e_1$ are
$$
\Pi_0h=T^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^4t_i\langle t_i,h\rangle
+M^{-1}\sum_{\alpha=2}^m z_\alpha\langle z_\alpha,h\rangle,
\qquad
\Pi_-h=\psi_-e_1\langle\psi_-e_1,h\rangle.
\tag{U.73b.4d.8}
$$
Translation and internal orthogonal transport give these projectors everywhere on $\mathcal M$. Its induced $L^2$ metric and volume are
$$
ds^2=T\sum_{i=1}^4 da_i^2+M\,ds_{S^{m-1}}^2,
\qquad
d\operatorname{vol}_{\mathrm{coll}}=T^2M^{(m-1)/2}\,d^4a\,d\Omega_{m-1}.
\tag{U.73b.4d.9}
$$
The compact internal factor is $O(m)/O(m-1)=S^{m-1}$, with total volume $2\pi^{m/2}M^{(m-1)/2}/\Gamma(m/2)$. For $m=1$, $S^0$ consists of the two signs and this is counting measure; there is no continuous internal zero mode. For $m=2$, writing $v=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ gives one compact fifth coordinate, $0\le\theta<2\pi$, of circumference $2\pi\sqrt M$. The full collective manifold also has the separate noncompact translation factor.

4. The action has the three distinct bihomogeneous weights $(2,2),(2,4),(p+1,4)$ of Theorem U.73b.3 and no weighted-dilation symmetry. Its amplitude--dilation block at $u e_1$, in the coordinates $(b,\tau)\mapsto e^b u(e^{-\tau}x)e_1$, is
$$
B=-(p-1)P
\begin{pmatrix}1&4/(p+1)\\4/(p+1)&4/(p+1)\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det B=-\frac{4(p-1)^2(3-p)}{(p+1)^2}P^2<0.
\tag{U.73b.4d.10}
$$
All three saddle term values are nonzero. Thus the extra $m-1$ kernel directions survive in the full Hessian while its amplitude--dilation block is invertible.

*Proof.* Write $q=p+1\in(2,4)$. The Sobolev embedding $H^1(\mathbb R^4)\subset L^q$ gives separate finiteness; conversely finite kinetic and positive-mass integrals already give the $H^1$ norm. For $F(z)=|z|^q/q$ on $\mathbb R^m$, its second derivative, defined as zero at $z=0$, is
$$
D^2F(z)=|z|^{q-2}I+(q-2)|z|^{q-4}zz^{\mathsf T}.
$$
This is continuous and has norm at most $(q-1)|z|^{q-2}$. Its substitution map is continuous from $L^q$ to $L^{q/(q-2)}$: convergence in $L^q$ implies convergence in measure and uniform integrability of the corresponding powers, which gives convergence in the indicated norm. Hölder's inequality then makes the second derivative continuous as a bilinear form on $L^q\times L^q$. Integrating the pointwise Taylor formula proves the claimed $C^2$ regularity on $H^1$, including fields that vanish. The Euler derivative is a $C^1$ map $X\to X^*=H^{-1}$.

For scalar existence, minimize
$$
c=\inf_{0\ne w\in H^1(\mathbb R^4)}
\frac{\int(|\nabla w|^2+\omega w^2)}{(\int|w|^q)^{2/q}}.
$$
Sobolev embedding gives $c>0$, and a nonzero smooth compactly supported test gives $c<\infty$. Taking absolute values and Schwarz rearrangements gives a nonnegative radial nonincreasing minimizing sequence $w_n$ with $\|w_n\|_q=1$ and bounded $H^1$ norm. For such functions, monotonicity gives $|w_n(r)|^2\le C r^{-4}\|w_n\|_2^2$. Consequently
$$
\int_{|x|>R}|w_n|^q\le C R^{-2(q-2)}
$$
uniformly in $n$. Rellich compactness on each ball, valid since $q<4$, and this tail bound give a subsequence converging strongly in $L^q$ and weakly in $H^1$ to a nonnegative radial nonincreasing minimizer $w$. Its Euler equation is $-\Delta w+\omega w=cw^{q-1}$, so $u=c^{1/(q-2)}w$ solves (U.73b.4d.2).

For clarity, the required regularity and decay follow within this argument. Local elliptic iteration starts from $u\in L^4$; while necessary the reciprocal integrability exponent changes by $1/r\mapsto p/r-1/2$. Since $p<3$, iteration reaches an exponent for which the nonlinear right side has integrability greater than $2$, giving boundedness by elliptic estimates and then $C^2$ regularity. The maximum principle gives $u>0$. The radial derivative is nonpositive. If $u'(r_0)=0$ at some $r_0>0$, then the nonpositive function $u'$ has a local maximum there, so $u''(r_0)=0$. Its linear radial equation and uniqueness with these zero initial data would make $u'$ identically zero. Hence $u'(r)<0$ for $r>0$. The radial initial equation similarly gives $u''(0)<0$. The $H^1$ radial bound gives $u(r)\to0$. For any $0<\gamma<\sqrt\omega$, outside a large ball one has $u^{p-1}\le\omega-\gamma^2$; comparison with a multiple of $e^{-\gamma r}$ for $-\Delta+\gamma^2$ gives exponential decay. Local elliptic estimates and the radial equation give exponential decay of the derivatives needed below. In particular $u\in H^3$, $x\cdot\nabla u\in H^2$, and all integrations by parts below have vanishing boundary terms. Scaling $u_{\omega,p}(x)=\omega^{1/(p-1)}u_{1,p}(\sqrt\omega x)$ reduces uniqueness of the positive radial decaying solution to precisely the whole-space case stated in Kwong's theorem.

Let $A(w)=\int(|\nabla w|^2+\omega w^2)$ and $C(w)=\int|w|^q$. Every nonzero ray has the unique Nehari representative $tw$, where $t^{q-2}=A(w)/C(w)$. On $A=C$,
$$
S(w)=\left(\frac12-\frac1q\right)A(w),
$$
and minimizing this is equivalent to minimizing $A/C^{2/q}$. Thus $u$ is a Nehari minimizer. The inequality $|\nabla|\Phi||\le|\nabla\Phi|$ makes the scalar and vector infima equal, attained by $uv$ for every constant unit vector $v$. Multiplication of the equation by $u$ gives $G+\omega M=P$. Differentiation under the spatial scaling, justified by the exponential bounds, gives $G+2\omega M=4P/q$. Solving these identities proves (U.73b.4d.4).

Differentiating the vector nonlinearity at $ue_1$ gives (U.73b.4d.5). Both potentials are bounded and tend to zero after the constant $\omega$ is removed. Their quadratic forms are therefore bounded perturbations of the closed free form on $H^1$, and their operators are the self-adjoint bounded perturbations of $-\Delta+\omega$ on $H^2$. Multiplication by either decaying potential is compact from $H^2$ to $L^2$: on a ball use Rellich compactness, and outside use its uniformly small sup norm. The resolvent identity consequently preserves the free essential spectrum $[\omega,\infty)$.

The transverse scalar operator satisfies $L_-u=0$ and, for compactly supported smooth $f$,
$$
\langle f,L_-f\rangle=\int u^2|\nabla(f/u)|^2\ge0.
$$
Density gives nonnegativity on $H^1$. If $L_-f=0$ with $f\in H^2$, choose cutoffs $\chi_R$ equal to one on the radius-$R$ ball, with $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. Testing the equation against $\chi_R^2f$ and using the preceding identity gives
$$
\int u^2|\nabla(\chi_Rf/u)|^2
=\int |\nabla\chi_R|^2 f^2\longrightarrow0.
$$
On each fixed ball $f/u$ therefore has zero weak gradient. It is constant on $\mathbb R^4$, so $\ker L_-=\mathbb Ru$.

For $L_+$, the scalar Nehari constraint $N(w)=A(w)-C(w)$ has derivative
$$
DN(u)[h]=-(p-1)\int u^p h.
$$
It is nonzero, and its zero space is a codimension-one tangent hyperplane. The minimum property and $DS(u)=0$ make the Hessian nonnegative there. A two-dimensional negative subspace would intersect this hyperplane nontrivially, a contradiction. Conversely
$$
\langle u,L_+u\rangle=-(p-1)P<0.
$$
Thus the full scalar operator has exactly one negative eigenvalue, counting multiplicity. Its bottom eigenfunction can be taken nonnegative by the variational principle and strictly positive by the maximum principle; simplicity follows already from the index bound. Rotational invariance and positivity then make its normalized eigenfunction radial. This proves the assertion about $\lambda_-$ and $\psi_-$.

We prove radial nondegeneracy rather than infer it from uniqueness. In spherical-harmonic sector $\ell$, the radial expression is
$$
\mathcal L_\ell=-\frac{d^2}{dr^2}-\frac3r\frac d{dr}
+\frac{\ell(\ell+2)}{r^2}+\omega-pu(r)^{p-1}
$$
on $L^2((0,\infty),r^3dr)$, with the regular radial realization inherited from $H^2(\mathbb R^4)$. The $\ell=0$ realization has one negative eigenvalue, since the negative test $u$ is radial. If it had a zero eigenfunction $z$, the Sturm oscillation theorem would give exactly one node $r_0>0$: the zero eigenvalue would be its second discrete eigenvalue below the threshold $\omega$. The relevant half-line problem is the usual separated radial Sturm problem; conjugation by $r^{3/2}$ gives the limit-point potential $3/(4r^2)+\omega-pu^{p-1}$, so eigenvalues below $\omega$ are simple and the node count applies.

The identities
$$
L_+u=-(p-1)u^p,
\qquad
L_+\left(\frac{u}{p-1}+\frac12x\cdot\nabla u\right)=-\omega u
$$
and self-adjointness imply $\langle z,u^p\rangle=\langle z,u\rangle=0$. Choose the sign of $z$ positive before $r_0$ and negative after it. Since $u$ is strictly decreasing,
$$
z(r)u(r)\bigl(u(r)^{p-1}-u(r_0)^{p-1}\bigr)>0
\quad(r\ne r_0).
$$
Its integral is nevertheless $\langle z,u^p\rangle-u(r_0)^{p-1}\langle z,u\rangle=0$, a contradiction. All integrals are finite by Cauchy--Schwarz and exponential decay of $u$. Thus $\mathcal L_0$ has no zero eigenfunction.

In the $\ell=1$ sector, $h=-u'>0$ solves $\mathcal L_1h=0$. The radial ground-state identity
$$
\int_0^\infty f\mathcal L_1f\,r^3dr
=\int_0^\infty h^2\left|(f/h)'\right|^2r^3dr
$$
first for test functions supported away from the endpoints, and then by form closure, proves nonnegativity. The regular solution space of the zero equation at the origin is one-dimensional: its regular solution is $O(r)$, whereas the other indicial behavior is $r^{-3}$ and is not in $L^2(r^3dr)$. Hence its kernel is exactly $\mathbb Rh$. For $\ell\ge2$ its quadratic form is that for $\ell=1$ plus
$$
\bigl(\ell(\ell+2)-3\bigr)\int_0^\infty |f|^2 r\,dr>0
\quad(f\ne0).
$$
The common form domain here is valid by the four-dimensional Hardy inequality. Thus those sectors have no kernel. The four degree-one spherical harmonics give precisely $\partial_i u$, proving the full scalar and then vector kernel (U.73b.4d.6).

All spectrum below $\omega$ consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, with possible accumulation only at $\omega$. The finite kernel just proved is therefore isolated, giving a strictly positive gap after removal of it and the sole negative eigenvalue. This proves (U.73b.4d.7) and the inverse bound. The spectral gap at zero gives closed range equal to $(\ker\mathcal H)^\perp$, with the claimed Fredholm kernel and cokernel; the graph norm is equivalent to the $H^2$ norm because the potential is bounded. This argument uses a gap below positive essential spectrum, rather than compact resolvent.

We now establish completeness of the critical orbit near each member in the full $H^1$ topology. Multiplication by the decaying potential is also compact $H^1\to H^{-1}$, by local $H^1\to L^2$ compactness and the small tail bound. Thus $\mathcal H:H^1\to H^{-1}$ is a Fredholm perturbation of the isomorphism $-\Delta+\omega$. Every weak kernel vector is in $H^2$, because the bounded potential times that vector is in $L^2$; its kernel is therefore the same finite space $K$ in (U.73b.4d.6). By symmetry, its range is the annihilator of $K$. The restriction from the $L^2$-orthogonal complement of $K$ in $H^1$ to that annihilator is an isomorphism.

Split a nearby field as $ue_1+k+n$, with $k\in K$ and $n\in H^1\cap K^\perp$, and project the Euler derivative onto the annihilator of $K$. The Banach implicit-function theorem gives a unique $C^1$ normal solution $n=n(k)$ near zero. The map $(a,v)\mapsto u(\cdot-a)v$ is $C^1$ into $H^1$; its differential at $(0,e_1)$ is the isomorphism from $\mathbb R^4\oplus T_{e_1}S^{m-1}$ onto $K$. Projection of this orbit onto $K$ is consequently a local diffeomorphism. Every orbit point solves the full Euler equation, so its normal component equals the unique $n(k)$. Any nearby critical point first solves the projected equation and is consequently that orbit point. For $m=1$ the same argument applies separately at each sign. Symmetry transports this conclusion to every member of $\mathcal M$.

Radiality gives $\int\partial_i u\partial_j u=\delta_{ij}G/4$; integration by parts gives $\int u\partial_i u=0$. These identities prove the orthogonality and projectors. For $dv\perp v$, differentiation of (U.73b.4d.3) gives $-v\,da\cdot\nabla u+u\,dv$, whose squared norm is $T|da|^2+M|dv|^2$. This proves the metric, its volume and the sphere-volume formula. The parametrization has no extra overlap: its modulus has its unique maximum at $a$, fixing the center, and division by $u(x-a)>0$ then fixes $v$. Finally the three saddle term values are $G/2,\omega M/2,-P/q$. Their outer products with the three displayed weights, simplified by (U.73b.4d.4), give (U.73b.4d.10). ∎

For fixed $p$, the spectral and normalization scales are exact. With the unitary dilation $(D_\omega f)(x)=\omega f(\sqrt\omega x)$ on four-dimensional $L^2$,
$$
L_{\pm,\omega}=\omega D_\omega L_{\pm,1}D_\omega^{-1},\quad
\lambda_{-,\omega}=\omega\lambda_{-,1},\quad
\delta_{\omega,p}=\omega\delta_{1,p},\quad
M_\omega=\omega^{2/(p-1)-2}M_1,\quad
T_\omega=\omega^{2/(p-1)-1}T_1.
$$
The parameters $p=1$ and $p=3$ are excluded. At $p=1$ the Fourier multiplier $|k|^2+\omega-1$ has no nonzero $L^2$ null vector. At $p=3$, the Nehari and Pohozaev identities would force $\omega M=0$, so a nonzero finite-energy solution is impossible for $\omega>0$.

<a id="corollary-u73b4e-bounded-below-local-potentials-preserving-the-power-saddle"></a>**Corollary U.73b.4e (Bounded-Below Local Potentials Preserving the Power Saddle).** In Theorem U.73b.4d choose $R>u(0)$ and a smooth function $\chi:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ equal to one on $[0,R]$ and zero on $[2R,\infty)$. Replace the local potential in (U.73b.4d.1) by
$$
\widetilde V(z)=\frac\omega2|z|^2-\frac1{p+1}\chi(|z|)|z|^{p+1}.
\tag{U.73b.4e.1}
$$
This is an $O(m)$-invariant $C^2$ potential with $\widetilde V(0)=0$, $D\widetilde V(0)=0$, $D^2\widetilde V(0)=\omega I$, and
$$
\widetilde V(z)\ge\frac\omega2|z|^2-\frac{(2R)^{p+1}}{p+1}.
$$
It is bounded below as a function of the local field value and grows quadratically at infinity. Its action is $C^2$ on $H^1$. The entire orbit (U.73b.4d.3), its action value, its full Hessian and domains, Morse index, kernel, normal gap, local critical-set completeness, projectors and collective metric remain exactly those in Theorem U.73b.4d.

*Proof.* Near zero the cut-off is constant, so the $C^2$ assertion follows from $p+1>2$; away from zero it is ordinary smooth calculus. The bound uses $0\le\chi\le1$ and its support. The cut-off nonlinear term and its first two derivatives have the same respective growth bounds $C|z|^{p+1}$, $C|z|^p$ and $C|z|^{p-1}$ as in the theorem, so the same Sobolev and Hölder proof gives $C^2$ action regularity and separate finite integrals. Every orbit field takes values with $|z|\le u(0)<R$, where the potential and its first two derivatives agree exactly with those of (U.73b.4d.1). Hence the Euler equation, saddle action and full Hessian agree. The implicit-function argument applies to the new $C^1$ Euler map with that same Hessian and the same exact orbit, proving local completeness. The projectors and metric depend only on the unchanged Hessian and orbit. The lower bound is a pointwise potential bound, rather than a lower bound on the action over an infinite spatial volume. ∎

The power family supplies a regular positive-mass vacuum and an $H^1$-local complete critical manifold for every $m$, with a compact fifth mode when $m=2$. Its essential spectrum and ordinary Sobolev domains distinguish it from the logarithmic oscillator family; Corollary U.73b.4e also places the same saddle in bounded-below local potentials. The internal symmetry here is global. Its use in Definition U.16b requires a specified PU gauge and response quotient under which the internal tangent survives, followed by the same-branch carrier marking, exponent calibration, determinant/remainder and physical-realization records.

<a id="theorem-u73b4f-a-local-single-scalar-false-vacuum-saddle-with-five-operator-zero-modes"></a>**Theorem U.73b.4f (A Local Single-Scalar False-Vacuum Saddle with Five Operator Zero Modes).** There is a smooth potential $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, bounded below and quadratic outside a compact interval, such that
$$
V(0)=V'(0)=0,\qquad V''(0)=1,\qquad \min_{\mathbb R}V<0.
\tag{U.73b.4f.1}
$$
The canonical local action, with ordinary Euclidean volume,
$$
S[\phi]=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\frac12|\nabla\phi|^2+V(\phi)\right)dx,
\qquad \phi\in H^1(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R),
\tag{U.73b.4f.2}
$$
is $C^2$ and has a smooth positive radial critical point $u$, with $u'(r)<0$ for $r>0$, $u'(0)=0$, and exponential decay. Its action is finite and positive. Its real $L^2$ Hessian
$$
H=-\Delta+V''(u),\qquad \operatorname{Dom}(H)=H^2(\mathbb R^4),
\tag{U.73b.4f.3}
$$
has Morse index one and exactly five zero modes:
$$
\ker H=\operatorname{span}\{-\partial_1u,-\partial_2u,-\partial_3u,-\partial_4u,z\},
\qquad z=z(r),\qquad \dim\ker H=5.
\tag{U.73b.4f.4}
$$
The radial mode $z$ has exactly one node and lies outside $\operatorname{span}\{u,r u'\}$. The amplitude--dilation restriction of the Hessian is nonsingular, with one negative and one positive eigenvalue. The essential spectrum of $H$ is $[1,\infty)$; after removing the negative eigenfunction and the five-dimensional kernel, its closed form has a strictly positive $L^2$ gap. Thus $H:H^2\to L^2$ is Fredholm of index zero, with kernel and cokernel dimension five.

Use this same $V$ in Definition U.6, with $\varepsilon_0>0$ and the actual $L_W$ of Proposition U.13a. The centered sample $u^*(r,i)=u(r)$ is an exact critical point. Its Friedrichs Hessian has Morse index one, kernel
$$
\operatorname{span}\{g(r)(x_i)_\mu:1\le\mu\le4\}
\oplus\operatorname{span}\{z(r)\mathbf1\},\qquad g=-u',
\tag{U.73b.4f.5}
$$
and a positive normal gap. The potential has exactly two local minima, separated by one local maximum. The construction below fixes $V$ by exact smooth functions, integrals and a variational spectral level; no target value enters these choices.

*Proof.* **I. The profiles and their potential.** Let $Q=u_{1,2}$ be the positive centered scalar ground state in Theorem U.73b.4d, and put $g_0=-Q'>0$ on $(0,\infty)$. Its equation is
$$
-Q''-\frac3rQ'+Q-Q^2=0.
\tag{U.73b.4f.6}
$$
That theorem gives smooth radial regularity, exponential decay of $Q$ and its derivatives, $g_0(r)=c r+O(r^3)$ with $c>0$, and exactly one negative radial eigenvalue and no radial zero for $-\Delta+1-2Q$. Smoothness of all orders here follows by elliptic iteration from the polynomial right side of (U.73b.4f.6).

The origin equation and $Q''(0)<0$ give $Q(0)>1$. Let $R>0$ be the unique radius with $Q(R)=1$, and write $h_0=r^3g_0$. Equation (U.73b.4f.6) gives
$$
h_0'(r)=r^3Q(r)(Q(r)-1),
$$
which is positive before $R$ and negative after $R$. We preserve this sign pattern while creating two separated radial negative tests.

Set
$$
\eta(s)=\begin{cases}e^{-1/s},&s>0,\\0,&s\le0,\end{cases}
\qquad
\theta(s)=\frac{\eta(s)}{\eta(s)+\eta(1-s)},
\qquad
T_{a,b}(r)=\theta\left(\frac{r-a}{b-a}\right)\quad(a<b).
$$
Thus $T_{a,b}$ is zero up to $a$, one from $b$ onwards, and nondecreasing. First define
$$
J_1=\int_{R/4}^{R/2}r^{-3}|T_{R/4,R/2}'(r)|^2dr,
\qquad
\epsilon=\min\left\{\frac R{128},
\left(\frac{45}{4096(J_1+R^{-4})}\right)^{1/4}\right\},
$$
and the disjoint cutoffs
$$
\chi_1=T_{\epsilon/4,\epsilon/2}(1-T_{R/4,R/2}),
\qquad
\chi_2=T_{5R/8,3R/4}(1-T_{4R,5R}).
$$
Put
$$
\begin{aligned}
D_1&=\int_{2\epsilon}^{4\epsilon}r^{-5}dr=\frac{15}{1024\epsilon^4},
& D_2&=\int_R^{2R}r^{-5}dr=\frac{15}{64R^4},\\
C_0&=\int_{\epsilon/4}^{\epsilon/2}h_0^2r^{-3}|\chi_1'|^2dr
+2\int_{R/4}^{R/2}h_0^2r^{-3}|\chi_1'|^2dr,
& A_1&=1+\sqrt{\frac{C_0}{3D_1-2J_1}},\\
C_2&=\int_{5R/8}^{3R/4}(h_0+A_1)^2r^{-3}|\chi_2'|^2dr
+\int_{4R}^{5R}h_0^2r^{-3}|\chi_2'|^2dr,
& A_2&=A_1+1+\sqrt{\frac{C_2}{3D_2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
These constants are finite and strictly positive. The choice of $\epsilon$ gives $3D_1\ge4(J_1+R^{-4})>2J_1$, so the definitions are valid. Define the smooth shoulder profile
$$
f=A_1T_{\epsilon,2\epsilon}
+(A_2-A_1)T_{7R/8,15R/16}
-A_2T_{2R,3R}.
\tag{U.73b.4f.7}
$$
It is nonnegative, supported in $[\epsilon,3R]$, equal to $A_1$ on $[2\epsilon,7R/8]$ and $A_2$ on $[15R/16,2R]$. Its derivative is nonnegative for $r<R$ and nonpositive for $r>R$.

For $0\le t\le1$ set
$$
h_t=h_0+t f,\qquad g_t=\frac{h_t}{r^3},\qquad
\nu_t(r)=\int_r^\infty g_t(s)\,ds
=Q(r)+t\int_r^\infty\frac{f(s)}{s^3}\,ds,
\qquad U_t=\nu_t(0),\qquad c_t=t\int_0^\infty\frac{f(s)}{s^3}\,ds.
\tag{U.73b.4f.8}
$$
Then $g_t>0$, $\nu_t'=-g_t$, $\nu_t=Q+c_t$ near the origin, and $\nu_t=Q$ for $r\ge3R$. Thus $\nu_t(|x|)$ is smooth, positive, strictly radially decreasing, and exponentially decaying. It maps $(0,\infty)$ bijectively onto $(0,U_t)$; write $r_t(s)$ for the inverse. On this field interval define
$$
F_t(s)=-g_t'(r_t(s))-\frac{3g_t(r_t(s))}{r_t(s)}
=-\frac{h_t'(r_t(s))}{r_t(s)^3}.
\tag{U.73b.4f.9}
$$
Near $s=0$ this is exactly $s-s^2$, since $\nu_t=Q$ on the tail. Near $U_t$ it is $(s-c_t)-(s-c_t)^2$, since $\nu_t=Q+c_t$ near the origin. The inverse function theorem handles every interior field value. Extend it smoothly to all real $s$ by
$$
F_t(s)=
\begin{cases}
(1-\theta(-s-1))(s-s^2)+\theta(-s-1)s,&s\le0,\\
(1-\theta(s-U_t-1))\big((s-c_t)-(s-c_t)^2\big)
+\theta(s-U_t-1)(s-U_t-3),&s\ge U_t,
\end{cases}
\qquad
V_t(s)=\int_0^sF_t(a)\,da.
\tag{U.73b.4f.10}
$$
The matching expressions hold on neighborhoods of the joins, proving smoothness. For $s\le-2$ the derivative is $s$, and for $s\ge U_t+2$ it is $s-U_t-3$, so $V_t$ is quadratic on both tails and bounded below. Near zero it is exactly $s^2/2-s^3/3$; hence $V_t(0)=V_t'(0)=0$ and $V_t''(0)=1$.

Moreover, $h_t'>0$ on $(0,R)$ and $h_t'<0$ on $(R,\infty)$. Consequently the only zero of $F_t$ in $(0,U_t)$ is $B_t=\nu_t(R)$; $F_t>0$ on $(0,B_t)$ and $F_t<0$ on $(B_t,U_t)$. On $s<0$ both terms in its defining blend are negative. On $U_t\le s\le U_t+2$, both terms used when the blend is nonconstant are negative, since $s-c_t\ge Q(0)>1$ and $s-U_t-3<0$. From $U_t+2$ onwards its unique zero is $M_t=U_t+3$, with positive derivative. Thus the complete critical-point list of $V_t$ is the two nondegenerate minima $0,M_t$ and the single maximum $B_t$. This maximum is also nondegenerate: $f$ is constant near $R$, and $h_t''(R)=h_0''(R)=R^3Q'(R)<0$ implies $V_t''(B_t)<0$. Reconstruction gives
$$
-\Delta\nu_t+V_t'(\nu_t)=0.
\tag{U.73b.4f.11}
$$

For each $t$, $V_t''$ and $V_t'''$ are bounded and $|V_t(s)|\le K_t s^2$. The action is therefore finite on $H^1$. Its first derivative is well defined because $|V_t'(s)|\le K_t'|s|$, and its second derivative is the usual kinetic form plus multiplication by $V_t''(\phi)$. The mean-value theorem and $H^1(\mathbb R^4)\subset L^4$ give
$$
\left|\int\bigl(V_t''(\phi)-V_t''(\psi)\bigr)hk\,dx\right|
\le\|V_t'''\|_\infty\|\phi-\psi\|_2\|h\|_4\|k\|_4.
\tag{U.73b.4f.12}
$$
The integral Taylor formula proves twice Fréchet differentiability and continuity of this second derivative on $H^1$. Equation (U.73b.4f.11), first against compactly supported tests and then by density, makes $\nu_t$ an $H^1$ critical point.

**II. Common operators and a controlled radial crossing.** Along this profile differentiation of (U.73b.4f.9) gives the bounded radial multiplier
$$
w_t(r):=V_t''(\nu_t(r))
=\frac{g_t''}{g_t}+\frac{3g_t'}{r g_t}-\frac3{r^2}.
\tag{U.73b.4f.13}
$$
Outside $[\epsilon,3R]$ this is $w_0=1-2Q$. In particular its apparent singularity at zero is removable. On $[\epsilon,3R]$ one has $g_t\ge g_0>0$ uniformly in $t$. Thus $w_t-w_0$ is a bounded smooth compactly supported radial function, depending Lipschitz-continuously on $t$ in the sup norm.

For $\lambda\ge0$ use the Friedrichs form closure from $C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$ on $\mathscr H_{\mathrm{rad}}=L^2((0,\infty),r^3dr)$:
$$
q_{\lambda,t}[f]=\int_0^\infty r^3\left(|f'|^2+
\left(w_t+\frac\lambda{r^2}\right)|f|^2\right)dr,
\qquad
\mathcal L_{\lambda,t}=-\partial_r^2-\frac3r\partial_r+w_t+\frac\lambda{r^2}.
\tag{U.73b.4f.14}
$$
The common form domain is the radial $H^1$ domain: the four-dimensional Hardy inequality bounds $\int r|f|^2dr$ by $\int r^3|f'|^2dr$. For each fixed $\lambda$, bounded multiplication gives a common operator domain as $t$ varies. For the continuum values $\lambda=\ell(\ell+2)$ these are precisely the radial realizations inherited from the $\ell$th spherical-harmonic sector of $H^2(\mathbb R^4)$.

The endpoint behavior of $g_t$ agrees with $g_0$, so $g_t$ belongs to every form domain in (U.73b.4f.14). Equation (U.73b.4f.13) gives $\mathcal L_{3,t}g_t=0$ in distributions and hence in the operator domain. Integration by parts for compactly supported $f=g_t h$ gives
$$
q_{3,t}[f]=\int_0^\infty r^3g_t^2|h'|^2dr\ge0,
\qquad
q_{\lambda,t}[f]=q_{3,t}[f]+(\lambda-3)\int_0^\infty r|f|^2dr.
\tag{U.73b.4f.15}
$$
Closure extends the identity in its closed-form sense. If $f\in\ker\mathcal L_{3,t}$, approximation in the form norm makes the nonnegative right side vanish locally; since $g_t$ is smooth and strictly positive on each compact subinterval, $(f/g_t)'=0$ there. Therefore
$$
\ker\mathcal L_{3,t}=\mathbb R g_t,\qquad
q_{0,t}[g_t]=-3\int_0^\infty r g_t^2dr<0.
\tag{U.73b.4f.16}
$$
The test $g_t\sim c r$ is legitimate in the radial form domain; it need not be a smooth radial scalar at the origin. For $\lambda>3$, (U.73b.4f.15) gives a nonnegative form with trivial kernel.

In the radial constant channel, the unitary map $f\mapsto r^{3/2}f$ gives the half-line expression
$$
-\partial_r^2+\frac{3}{4r^2}+w_t(r).
\tag{U.73b.4f.17}
$$
At zero this is limit point: the two leading solutions of the radial equation are constant and $r^{-2}$, and only the first is in $L^2(r^3dr)$. Infinity is also limit point. The bounded perturbation of the regular radial realization has essential spectrum $[1,\infty)$, because $w_t-1$ tends to zero and multiplication by it is compact from the radial $H^2$ domain to $L^2$, by local Rellich compactness and its small sup norm on the tail. Eigenvalues below $1$ are simple, with the usual Sturm node count.

Define the second variational level, including the possibility of the essential edge,
$$
\mu_2(t)=\inf_{\substack{E\subset\operatorname{Dom}(q_{0,t})\\\dim E=2}}
\ \sup_{0\ne f\in E}\frac{q_{0,t}[f]}{\|f\|_{\mathrm{rad}}^2}.
\tag{U.73b.4f.18}
$$
If there is only one eigenvalue below $1$, this level is $1$; otherwise it is the second discrete eigenvalue. At $t=0$, Theorem U.73b.4d gives one negative eigenvalue and no radial zero. Its zero gap and essential threshold imply $\mu_2(0)>0$. Since the domains are common,
$$
|\mu_2(t)-\mu_2(s)|\le\|w_t-w_s\|_\infty.
\tag{U.73b.4f.19}
$$
At $t=1$ take $v_i=g_1\chi_i$. Their supports are disjoint. The ground-state identity becomes
$$
q_{3,1}[v_i]=\int_0^\infty h_1^2r^{-3}|\chi_i'|^2dr,
\qquad
q_{0,1}[v_i]=q_{3,1}[v_i]-3\int_0^\infty h_1^2r^{-5}\chi_i^2dr.
$$
In the first left transition $f=0$, while throughout its right transition $f=A_1$. Using $(h_0+A_1)^2\le2h_0^2+2A_1^2$ gives $q_{3,1}[v_1]\le C_0+2A_1^2J_1$. On $[2\epsilon,4\epsilon]$, $\chi_1=1$ and $h_1\ge A_1$. In the second left transition $f=A_1$, while throughout its right transition $f=0$, so $q_{3,1}[v_2]=C_2$, independent of $A_2$. On $[R,2R]$, $\chi_2=1$ and $h_1\ge A_2$. Therefore the exact choices above give
$$
q_{0,1}[v_1]\le C_0-A_1^2(3D_1-2J_1)<0,
\qquad
q_{0,1}[v_2]\le C_2-3A_2^2D_2<0.
\tag{U.73b.4f.20}
$$
All cross form and inner-product terms vanish. Their two-dimensional span is negative definite, proving $\mu_2(1)<0$.

The exact choice
$$
t_*:=\min\{t\in[0,1]:\mu_2(t)\le0\}
\tag{U.73b.4f.21}
$$
therefore satisfies $0<t_*<1$ and $\mu_2(t_*)=0$. This is a discrete eigenvalue below the essential threshold. Equation (U.73b.4f.16) gives at least one strictly negative eigenvalue at this parameter; the second variational level and Sturm simplicity give exactly one negative eigenvalue and exactly one radial zero. Denote its real eigenfunction by $z$. It has exactly one node. From now on set $u=\nu_{t_*}$, $g=g_{t_*}$ and $V=V_{t_*}$.

**III. The full scalar and sampled spectra.** The bounded multiplier $V''(u)$ makes (U.73b.4f.3) a self-adjoint bounded perturbation of $-\Delta+1$ on $H^2$. Its form domain is $H^1$. Multiplication by $V''(u)-1$ is compact $H^2\to L^2$ by the same local and tail argument, giving essential spectrum $[1,\infty)$. Spherical harmonics split its form into (U.73b.4f.14) with $\lambda=\ell(\ell+2)$. The $\ell=0$ channel has the negative eigenvalue and the single zero just proved. The $\ell=1$ channel has kernel $\mathbb Rg$ times the four degree-one harmonics, and no negative direction. Every $\ell\ge2$ channel is nonnegative with no zero by (U.73b.4f.15). This proves (U.73b.4f.4) and the full index one. Elliptic regularity places the radial zero in $H^2$, and then in every local Sobolev space; its regular radial representative is smooth at the origin.

Every spectral point below the positive essential threshold is an isolated eigenvalue of finite multiplicity, with accumulation possible only at the threshold. Consequently there is $\delta>0$ such that, for the normalized negative eigenfunction $\psi_-$,
$$
\langle h,Hh\rangle\ge\delta\|h\|_2^2
\quad\text{if }h\in H^1,\quad h\perp\ker H,\quad h\perp\psi_-.
\tag{U.73b.4f.22}
$$
The form notation on the left applies to every such $h$. The isolated finite kernel gives closed range $(\ker H)^\perp$ on the graph domain, which is equivalent to $H^2$ because the multiplier is bounded. This proves the Fredholm and normal-inverse assertions.

The actual sampled angular spectrum and multiplicities are
$$
\sigma(L_W)=\{0^1,3^4,8^9,15^8,24^2\}.
$$
Since $L_W\mathbf1=0$, the centered sample satisfies the full sampled Euler equation. With the normalized angular inner product of Theorem U.13b its Hessian is
$$
\mathcal H_{\mathrm{samp}}
=\frac1{\varepsilon_0}
\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\{0,3,8,15,24\}}
\left(\mathcal L_{\lambda,t_*}\otimes I_{E_\lambda}\right).
\tag{U.73b.4f.23}
$$
These angular values are continuum values for $\ell=0,1,2,3,4$. The corresponding continuum radial restrictions therefore supply exactly the same index and kernel counts, and each has essential threshold $1$. The finite direct sum has threshold $1/\varepsilon_0$, a finite isolated kernel and a positive normal gap. Corollary U.13a.1 identifies the four coordinate vectors with $E_3$ and the constant vector spans $E_0$, proving (U.73b.4f.5). Its radial saddle action is $S[u]/(2\pi^2\varepsilon_0)>0$.

**IV. False vacuum, positive action and the shape direction.** For every member of the reconstructed family the mechanical energy obeys
$$
\frac d{dr}\left(\frac12g_t^2-V_t(\nu_t)\right)
=-\frac3r g_t^2.
$$
Its limiting value at infinity is zero, and at zero it is $-V_t(U_t)$. The endpoint bounds make the integral convergent, so
$$
V_t(U_t)=-3\int_0^\infty\frac{g_t(r)^2}{r}\,dr<0.
\tag{U.73b.4f.24}
$$
Since $V_t$ decreases strictly from $U_t$ to $M_t$, (U.73b.4f.24) gives $V_t(M_t)<0$. The critical-point classification and quadratic growth make $M_t$ the unique global minimum. Thus zero is a positive-mass false vacuum separated from the lower true vacuum by exactly one barrier.

Write $G=\int|\nabla u|^2>0$ and $P=\int V(u)$. The exponentially decaying smooth field makes the spatial scaling $u(e^{-\tau}x)$ twice differentiable in $H^1$. Its action is $e^{2\tau}G/2+e^{4\tau}P$. Criticality gives $G+4P=0$, hence
$$
S[u]=\frac14G>0,\qquad
\langle r u',H(r u')\rangle=-2G<0.
\tag{U.73b.4f.25}
$$
All integrals are finite. On $r\ge3R$, $u=Q$ and $H=-\Delta+1-2Q$, so direct differentiation of (U.73b.4f.6) gives
$$
H Q=-Q^2,\qquad H(rQ')=-2Q+2Q^2.
\tag{U.73b.4f.26}
$$
If $a u+b r u'$ were in the full kernel, this tail identity would imply $-2b+(2b-a)Q(r)=0$ for every $r\ge3R$. Strict decrease of $Q$ forces $a=b=0$. In particular $z$ is a genuine radial shape direction outside that two-plane.

For completeness, let $B$ be the full Hessian form and $d=r u'$. In a form with one negative direction, the $B$-orthogonal complement of a vector with $B(d,d)<0$ is nonnegative, and its zero vectors are exactly the full kernel. To verify this directly, decompose $d=a\psi_-+d_++d_0$ and $h=c\psi_-+h_++h_0$ into negative, positive and zero spectral spaces, writing the negative eigenvalue as $-\kappa$. Here $a\ne0$ and $B(d_+,d_+)<\kappa a^2$. If $B(h,d)=0$, Cauchy--Schwarz in the positive form gives
$$
\kappa c^2\le\frac{B(d_+,d_+)}{\kappa a^2}B(h_+,h_+),
\qquad
B(h,h)\ge\left(1-\frac{B(d_+,d_+)}{\kappa a^2}\right)B(h_+,h_+)\ge0.
$$
Equality forces $h_+=0$ and $c=0$, leaving precisely a kernel vector. Apply this to the nonzero vector obtained by subtracting a multiple of $d$ from $u$ to make it $B$-orthogonal to $d$. The tail calculation excludes its membership in the full kernel, so its form value is strictly positive. Thus the amplitude--dilation block has signature $(-,+)$ and is nonsingular. ∎

<a id="corollary-u73b4g-complete-operator-nullity-alternatives-on-the-monotone-scalar-source"></a>**Corollary U.73b.4g (Complete Operator-Nullity Alternatives on the Monotone Scalar Source).** Let $V$ and $u$ satisfy the qualitative false-vacuum, monotone one-bounce and endpoint hypotheses of Lemmas U.13a.2--U.13a.3, without assuming the radial gap record $\mathfrak C_{U,0}$. Put $m^2=V''(0)>0$. For the continuum scalar Hessian on $H^2(\mathbb R^4)$ and the actual sampled Hessian of Definition U.6,
$$
\dim\ker H=\dim\ker\mathcal H_{\mathrm{samp}}
=4+\dim\ker\mathcal L_0\in\{4,5\}.
\tag{U.73b.4g.1}
$$
The orthogonal complement of the translation span in either kernel is spanned by a radial vector whenever it is nonzero. The alternatives have an exact matching criterion: let $w$ be the regular solution of $\mathcal L_0w=0$ with $w(0)=1$, $w'(0)=0$, and let $v_\infty$ be the solution normalized by $r^{3/2}e^{mr}v_\infty(r)\to1$ at infinity. Then, for any $a>0$,
$$
\dim\ker H=5
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal W:=a^3\bigl(w(a)v_\infty'(a)-w'(a)v_\infty(a)\bigr)=0.
\tag{U.73b.4g.2}
$$
The same criterion decides the sampled nullity. Both values occur with Morse index one, smooth one-barrier potentials and a lower true vacuum in the family of Theorem U.73b.4f.

*Proof.* The attained field interval is compact, so $V''(u)$ is bounded and tends to $m^2$. The endpoint record and $u(\infty)=0$ imply $u(r)=\int_r^\infty(-u'(s))ds=O(e^{-\mu r})$. Since $V\in C^3$, $V''(u)-m^2$ also decays exponentially. The continuum Hessian is self-adjoint on $H^2$, with form domain $H^1$ and essential spectrum $[m^2,\infty)$, by bounded perturbation and the local Rellich and tail argument in Theorem U.73b.4f. Lemma U.13a.3 supplies the nonnegative $\lambda=3$ channel with its simple radial ground zero $g=-u'$ and excludes every $\lambda>3$ kernel. The four degree-one harmonics give the continuum translation kernel. The actual sampled eigenvalues and multiplicities give the same four-dimensional contribution and the same $\lambda=0$ channel. Limit-point radial Sturm theory gives $\dim\ker\mathcal L_0\le1$, proving (U.73b.4g.1).

The regular radial solution exists uniquely from the integral equation
$$
w(r)=1+\int_0^r s^{-3}\int_0^s \tau^3 V''(u(\tau))w(\tau)\,d\tau\,ds.
$$
Its locally independent solution has leading behavior $r^{-2}$ and is not in $L^2(r^3dr)$ near zero. For the tail, put $Z(r)=3/(4r^2)+V''(u(r))-m^2$, which is integrable on every sufficiently remote half-line. Writing $v_\infty=r^{-3/2}e^{-mr}k$ gives the Volterra equation
$$
k(r)=1+\int_r^\infty\frac{1-e^{-2m(s-r)}}{2m}Z(s)k(s)\,ds.
\tag{U.73b.4g.3}
$$
On a sufficiently remote half-line its integral operator has sup norm less than one. Contraction therefore gives the unique bounded solution there, with $k(r)\to1$; the ordinary differential equation extends it to every $r>0$. Reduction of order gives the independent growing solution with leading behavior $r^{-3/2}e^{mr}/(2m)$, so every square-integrable tail solution is proportional to $v_\infty$.

Abel's identity makes $r^3(wv_\infty'-w'v_\infty)$ constant. It vanishes exactly when the regular solution and the decaying solution are proportional. In that case their common solution lies in the Friedrichs form and operator domain at both endpoints; otherwise no radial zero eigenfunction exists. This proves (U.73b.4g.2). In Theorem U.73b.4f, $t=0$ retains the nondegenerate scalar power Hessian and $t=t_*$ has the single radial zero. Both reconstructed potentials have the stated one-barrier geometry and index one, proving attainment of both alternatives. ∎

The Wronskian criterion is an exact spectral characterization; certifying its vanishing or nonvanishing for an arbitrary supplied potential is a separate analytic or validated-computation task.

This construction supplies a canonical local single-scalar example for the nonbihomogeneous shape kernel: positive mass and Morse index one coexist with exactly one additional radial operator zero. Its one-barrier potential and monotone finite-action profile satisfy the qualitative false-vacuum and endpoint hypotheses of Lemmas U.13a.2--U.13a.3, while its radial zero prevents acceptance of the independent no-zero record (U.13a.2d). Thus the radial gap record is an independent hypothesis of Theorem U.13b, rather than a consequence of its qualitative bounce assumptions. The four continuum translations are exact moduli. Integration of the additional radial zero at fixed $V$, and integration of the sampled translation-shaped vectors, are separate nonlinear questions; operator nullity five alone supplies neither a five-dimensional Morse--Bott collective-coordinate Jacobian nor a $\lambda^{5/2}$ prefactor. A compact fifth collective coordinate under Definition U.16b requires that nonlinear integration and the stated physical quotient and branch certificates. Carrier marking, exponent calibration and cosmological realization retain their own records.

<a id="theorem-u73b4h-no-compact-fifth-critical-circle-for-a-canonical-real-scalar"></a>**Theorem U.73b.4h (No Compact Fifth Critical Circle for a Canonical Real Scalar).** Fix one real potential $V\in C^2(\mathbb R)$, with $V(0)=V'(0)=0$, and the translation- and rotation-invariant action
$$
 S[u]=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\tfrac12|\nabla u|^2+V(u)\right)\,dx.
$$
Consider its nonzero real classical critical points $u$, so $-\Delta u+V'(u)=0$. The boundary condition is decay to the fixed vacuum zero at spatial infinity. Assume that $u$ is $C^3$ and that, for some constants $C,\gamma>0$ depending on $u$,
$$
 |D^\alpha u(x)|\le C e^{-\gamma|x|}\qquad(|\alpha|\le3).
 \tag{U.73b.4h.1}
$$
Use the real Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb R^4,dx)$, form domain $H^1$, and full Hessian
$$
 H_u=-\Delta+V''(u),\qquad D(H_u)=H^2(\mathbb R^4).
 \tag{U.73b.4h.2}
$$
The action and its first variation are used on the declared localized fields and compactly supported variations; these are continuum domains without angular sampling. Since $u$ is bounded, $V''(u)$ is a bounded real multiplier, so (U.73b.4h.2) is self-adjoint on exactly the displayed domain. The decay hypothesis makes the action finite because $V(t)=O(t^2)$ at zero. It also admits all translation and rotation tangents into this same operator domain.

1. **Low nullity forces radiality.** If $\dim\ker H_u\le5$, then $u$ is radial about its uniquely defined square-density center
$$
   c(u)=\frac{\int x\,u(x)^2\,dx}{\int u(x)^2\,dx}.
   \tag{U.73b.4h.3}
$$
   Neither positivity nor monotonicity of $u$, a prescribed Morse index, or a radial ansatz is assumed.

2. **No compact fifth circle.** There is no continuous injective family, indexed by $S^1$, of translation classes of such critical points for this same $V$, all having Hessian nullity at most five. Here continuity means that the uniquely centered representatives
   $\widehat u(x)=u(x+c(u))$ vary continuously in $C^0_{\mathrm{loc}}$; for example, local $C^0$ convergence together with convergence in the weighted space $L^2((1+|x|)dx)$ suffices. Consequently this scalar class cannot furnish the compact fifth factor in a five-dimensional Morse–Bott component of Definition U.16b for which the same five-dimensional kernel condition holds along the whole circle. A condition imposed only at one reference point is not sufficient for this corollary: a circle encountering higher-nullity points is not excluded.

3. The same exclusion holds when $V$ is even and translation classes are further identified by the vacuum-preserving sign symmetry $u\sim-u$.

*Proof.* **I. The admitted symmetry tangents and the translation slice.** Set $M=\int u^2>0$. Differentiating the Euler equation and its rotational covariance gives
$$
 H_u(-\partial_i u)=0,\qquad
 H_u\bigl(-(Ax)\cdot\nabla u\bigr)=0
 \quad(A\in\mathfrak {so}(4)).
 \tag{U.73b.4h.4}
$$
The derivatives through order three in (U.73b.4h.1) put both kinds of tangent in $H^2$, including the factors of $x$ in the rotation tangent. Thus these are operator-kernel equations, not only quadratic-form identities. The four translation tangents are independent: if $b\cdot\nabla u=0$ for a nonzero constant $b$, then $u$ is constant along every line parallel to $b$; its decay, or its $L^2$ norm, forces $u=0$, contrary to the premise.

Translate the field so that $c(u)=0$. The bounded linear functional
$$
 \Lambda_u(h)=\frac2M\int x\,u(x)h(x)\,dx\in\mathbb R^4
 \tag{U.73b.4h.5}
$$
is defined for every $h\in L^2$, because $xu\in L^2$. It is the differential of the center on the symmetry families. Integration by parts, with all boundary terms vanishing by (U.73b.4h.1), gives
$$
 \Lambda_u(-\partial_i u)=e_i,\qquad
 \Lambda_u\bigl(-(Ax)\cdot\nabla u\bigr)
   =\frac1M\int Ax\,u^2\,dx=0.
 \tag{U.73b.4h.6}
$$
Consequently $\Lambda_u$ has rank four on $\ker H_u$, while the rotation-tangent space lies in its kernel. The nullity bound yields
$$
 \dim\operatorname{span}\{(Ax)\cdot\nabla u:A\in\mathfrak {so}(4)\}\le1.
 \tag{U.73b.4h.7}
$$
This calculation keeps the physical translation directions; centering is a coordinate choice, not removal of those four zero modes from the Hessian count.

**II. A one-dimensional rotation orbit is impossible.** Let
$$
 \mathfrak h=\{A\in\mathfrak {so}(4):(Ax)\cdot\nabla u=0\}.
$$
It is the stabilizer Lie algebra. Indeed, the vanishing derivative says that $u$ is constant along the flow $x\mapsto e^{tA}x$, hence fixed by that one-parameter group. The $C^1$ orbit map in $L^2$ has differential $A\mapsto-(Ax)\cdot\nabla u$; its kernel is $\mathfrak h$. Equation (U.73b.4h.7) makes $\mathfrak h$ have codimension at most one.

For completeness, a compact perfect Lie algebra has no codimension-one subalgebra. Equip $\mathfrak {so}(4)$ with its positive invariant inner product $\langle A,B\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(AB)$. If $\mathfrak h$ had codimension one, choose nonzero $X\perp\mathfrak h$. For $Y,Z\in\mathfrak h$, invariance and closure of $\mathfrak h$ give

$$
\langle[Y,X],Z\rangle=-\langle X,[Y,Z]\rangle=0.
$$

Skew-adjointness of $\operatorname{ad}Y$ also gives $\langle[Y,X],X\rangle=0$. Therefore $[Y,X]=0$. It follows that every bracket of two elements of $\mathfrak {so}(4)=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathbb RX$ lies in $\mathfrak h$. This contradicts perfection: the elementary skew matrices satisfy $E_{ij}=[E_{ik},E_{kj}]$ for a third distinct index $k$, so their brackets span $\mathfrak {so}(4)$. Hence $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak {so}(4)$. Connectedness of $SO(4)$ makes $u$ invariant under every rotation about its center. This proves Part 1.

**III. A centered radial solution has one real initial datum.** Write a centered solution as $u(x)=f(|x|)$. Regularity gives $f'(0)=0$, and the radial equation is
$$
 f''+\frac3r f'=V'(f),\qquad
 f(r)=a+\int_0^r s^{-3}\int_0^s t^3 V'(f(t))\,dt\,ds,
 \quad a=f(0).
 \tag{U.73b.4h.8}
$$
If $f,g$ have the same $a$, choose a local interval of field values containing both profiles and a Lipschitz constant $L$ for $V'$ there. Their difference satisfies
$$
 \sup_{0\le t\le r}|f(t)-g(t)|
 \le\frac{Lr^2}{8}\sup_{0\le t\le r}|f(t)-g(t)|.
 \tag{U.73b.4h.9}
$$
For sufficiently small $r$ the factor is less than one, so the profiles agree there. Ordinary differential-equation uniqueness on every interval away from zero extends agreement to all radii on which both solutions exist. Thus the central value $a$ determines the full centered solution. In particular $a=0$ would yield the identically zero solution, which is excluded.

By Part 1, a hypothetical circle of translation classes has radial centered representatives. The map
$$
 [u]\longmapsto \widehat u(0)=u(c(u))\in\mathbb R
 \tag{U.73b.4h.10}
$$
is continuous by the stated topology, and injective by (U.73b.4h.8)–(U.73b.4h.9). A continuous injection from the compact circle into the Hausdorff line would be a homeomorphism onto a compact connected subset of the line. A nonconstant such subset is a closed interval. Removing an interior point disconnects that interval, whereas removing any point leaves the circle connected, a contradiction. This proves Part 2. Equivalently, wherever a regular one-dimensional centered critical manifold exists, its central value is a separating real coordinate, so that manifold cannot close into a circle.

If $V$ is even, uniqueness also shows that central values $a$ and $-a$ give precisely opposite profiles. Therefore $[u]\mapsto|u(c(u))|$ is continuous and injective after the sign identification, and the same argument applies. A smooth internal field reparametrization preserving the canonical kinetic term has derivative of magnitude one; preserving the distinguished vacuum zero leaves only the identity and sign. This proves Part 3. ∎

Theorem U.73b.4h excludes a compact fifth critical circle on the canonical single-real-scalar continuum class; it does not exclude a fifth operator zero, which Theorem U.73b.4f realizes. Such a zero may be isolated, may integrate along a noncompact family or may meet a singular critical set; in this class it cannot integrate into a circle along which the full Hessian nullity stays at most five, so a proposed circle must leave one of the fixed-potential, localization, canonical-scalar, regularity, ordinary-quotient or nullity hypotheses. The two-component compact internal circles of Theorems U.73b.4b and U.73b.4d are unaffected: their radial initial data are vector-valued and trace a circle. The sampled angular action of Definition U.6 lies outside the theorem because it does not carry the continuum $SO(4)$ action.

<a id="corollary-u73b4i-nullity-classification-for-on-invariant-multicomponent-bounces"></a>**Corollary U.73b.4i (Nullity Classification for $O(N)$-Invariant Multicomponent Bounces).** Let $V$ and $u$ satisfy the hypotheses of Corollary U.73b.4g, put $m^2=V''(0)$, and let $N\ge2$. On fields $\Phi:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^N$ consider the $O(N)$-invariant canonical action
$$
S_N[\Phi]=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\Bigl(\frac12|\nabla\Phi|^2+V(|\Phi|)\Bigr)dx .
\tag{U.73b.4i.1}
$$
The potential $z\mapsto V(|z|)$ is $C^2$ on $\mathbb R^N$, since $V'(0)=0$ makes its Hessian $V''(|z|)\hat z\hat z^{\mathsf T}+|z|^{-1}V'(|z|)(I-\hat z\hat z^{\mathsf T})$ tend to $m^2I$ at $z=0$. Fix a unit vector $e\in\mathbb R^N$. Then $\Phi_*=ue$ is a critical point, and its Hessian on $L^2(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^N)$, with domain $H^2(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^N)$, is
$$
\mathcal H_N=L_+\otimes ee^{\mathsf T}+L_-\otimes(I-ee^{\mathsf T}),\qquad
L_+=-\Delta+V''(u),\qquad L_-=-\Delta+\frac{V'(u)}{u}.
\tag{U.73b.4i.2}
$$

1. $L_-\ge0$, $\ker L_-=\mathbb Ru$, and the essential spectrum of $L_-$ is $[m^2,\infty)$. Consequently
$$
\ker\mathcal H_N=(\ker L_+)\,e\ \oplus\ \{u\,a:a\in\mathbb R^N,\ a\perp e\},
\qquad
\dim\ker\mathcal H_N=4+\dim\ker\mathcal L_0+(N-1),
\tag{U.73b.4i.3}
$$
where $\mathcal L_0$ is the radial operator of Corollary U.73b.4g, and the negative index of $\mathcal H_N$ equals that of the scalar Hessian $L_+$.
2. The vectors $ua$, $a\perp e$, are the tangents at $\Phi_*$ of the orbit $\{uv:v\in S^{N-1}\}$ of exact critical points, and they are orthogonal to the four translation vectors $-\partial_\mu u\,e$.
3. $\dim\ker\mathcal H_N=5$ exactly when $N=2$ and the Wronskian $\mathcal W$ of (U.73b.4g.2) is nonzero. The kernel is then the tangent space at $\Phi_*$ of the family $\{u(\cdot-a)v:a\in\mathbb R^4,\ v\in S^1\}$ of exact critical points, whose internal factor is a compact circle.

*Proof.* Since $u>0$, the Hessian of $z\mapsto V(|z|)$ at $z=u(x)e$ is $V''(u)ee^{\mathsf T}+u^{-1}V'(u)(I-ee^{\mathsf T})$. Writing a compactly supported variation as $\xi e+\chi$ with $\chi\perp e$, the second variation of (U.73b.4i.1) at $\Phi_*$ is therefore $\int(|\nabla\xi|^2+V''(u)\xi^2+|\nabla\chi|^2+u^{-1}V'(u)|\chi|^2)\,dx$, whose operator is (U.73b.4i.2). The critical-point equation $-\Delta u+V'(u)=0$ gives criticality of $ue$ and $L_-u=0$. The multiplier $u^{-1}V'(u)$ is continuous and bounded, because $V'(s)/s\to m^2$ as $s\downarrow0$, and $u^{-1}V'(u)-m^2$ tends to zero at infinity; as in the proof of Theorem U.73b.4d, $L_-$ is therefore a self-adjoint bounded perturbation of $-\Delta+m^2$ on $H^2$ with essential spectrum $[m^2,\infty)$. For compactly supported smooth $f$, the identity $u^{-1}V'(u)=u^{-1}\Delta u$ gives
$$
\langle f,L_-f\rangle=\int u^2\,|\nabla(f/u)|^2\,dx\ge0 ,
$$
and the cutoff argument of Theorem U.73b.4d gives $\ker L_-=\mathbb Ru$. The operator (U.73b.4i.2) is diagonal in the decomposition $\mathbb R^N=\mathbb Re\oplus e^\perp$, so its kernel is $(\ker L_+)e\oplus(\ker L_-)\otimes e^\perp$, and Corollary U.73b.4g gives $\dim\ker L_+=4+\dim\ker\mathcal L_0$. Nonnegativity of $L_-$ leaves the negative index to $L_+$. This proves item 1.

For item 2, the curves $\cos\theta\,ue+\sin\theta\,ua$, $|a|=1$, $a\perp e$, consist of critical points by $O(N)$ invariance, and $\langle ua,\partial_\mu u\,e\rangle=(a\cdot e)\int u\,\partial_\mu u\,dx=0$. For item 3, (U.73b.4i.3) equals $5$ exactly when $\dim\ker\mathcal L_0+N=2$; since $N\ge2$, this means $N=2$ and $\ker\mathcal L_0=\{0\}$, which by (U.73b.4g.2) is $\mathcal W\ne0$. The kernel is then spanned by the four translation vectors and $ue^\perp$, which are the tangents of the displayed family. ∎

For $N=2$ and $\mathcal W\ne0$ the kernel identity (U.16b.1) holds with a compact one-parameter internal orbit; the completeness of the critical set near that orbit is proved for the power family in Theorem U.73b.4d and Corollary U.73b.4e. The internal rotation is a global symmetry of $S_N$; its use in Definition U.16b requires the PU gauge and response quotient under which $ue^\perp$ survives.

### U.73b.5 Exact Logarithmic Saddle, Absolute Determinant and False-Vacuum Boundary

<a id="proposition-u73b5-four-mode-logarithmic-comparison-model-and-its-exact-scope"></a>**Proposition U.73b.5 (Four-Mode Logarithmic Comparison Model and Its Exact Scope).** Take the already defined $D=4,m=1$ logarithmic comparison action, transported to the Definition U.4/U.6 normalization with $\varepsilon=\log2$. The actual sampled saddle has one negative mode and four zero modes, the complete spectrum and absolute positive determinant below, and an explicit rank-$288$ reducing Feshbach projection. Its natural sampled translations fail to be critical, and its zero field has no finite quadratic false-vacuum Hessian. These statements concern this specified comparison action. They do not refute another smooth action satisfying the complete four-mode relative-determinant and real-stress chain.

**Proof and source normalization.**

Use the scalar potential

$$
V(q)=-(1/2)q^2(\log q^2+3),\quad V(0)=0,
$$

and $\varepsilon=\ln 2$. Definition U.4 fixes $S_{\mathrm{cont}}=(2\pi^2\varepsilon)^{-1}\int[|\nabla\phi|^2/2+V(\phi)]\,d^4x$. Definition U.6 uses the normalized 24-vertex angular average and the same $\varepsilon$. The U.73 action before this transport has no $(2\pi^2\varepsilon)^{-1}$ factor: its saddle value $\pi^2/2$ must not be silently retained as the value of $S_{\mathrm{disc}}$.

**Exact saddle and exponent.**

Let $g(r)=\exp(-r^2/2)$ and $u^*(r,i)=g(r)$. Since $V'(q)=-q(\log q^2+4)$, the radial equation is

$$
-g''-3g'/r+V'(g)=0.
$$

The discrete angular first variation vanishes on the constant angular vector. Thus $u^*$ is an actual critical point against compactly supported sampled variations, and its compact-test second variation has the closed realization below. No global $C^2$ neighborhood containing the false vacuum is claimed.

Its radial action is exactly

$$
\Delta S=(1/\varepsilon)\int_0^\infty r^3 \exp(-r^2)(r^2-3/2)\,dr=1/(4\varepsilon).
$$

On the separately imported $\lambda_*=2$ residual-budget convention, the weight exponent is

$$
B=\lambda_*\Delta S=1/(2 \ln 2)=0.721347520444481704\ldots .
$$
